paper_metadata.title: The Deep Arbitrary Polynomial Chaos Neural Network or how Deep Artificial Neural Networks could benefit from Data-Driven Homogeneous Chaos Theory
paper_metadata.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Machine learning have been widely used in various fields of mathematical computing, physical modeling, computational science, communication science, and stochastic analysis. Approaches based on Deep Artificial Neural Networks (DANN) are very popular in our days. Depending on the learning task, the exact form of DANNs is determined via their multi-layer architecture, activation functions and the so-called loss function. However, for a majority of deep learning approaches based on DANNs, the kernel structure of neural signal processing remains the same, where the node response is encoded as a linear superposition of neural activity, while the non-linearity is triggered by the activation functions. In the current paper, we suggest to analyze the neural signal processing in DANNs from the point of view of homogeneous chaos theory as known from polynomial chaos expansion (PCE). From the PCE perspective, the (linear) response on each node of a DANN could be seen as a $1^{st}$ degree multi-variate polynomial of single neurons from the previous layer, i.e. linear weighted sum of monomials. From this point of view, the conventional DANN structure relies implicitly (but erroneously) on a Gaussian distribution of neural signals. Additionally, this view revels that by design DANNs do not necessarily fulfill any orthogonality or orthonormality condition for a majority of data-driven applications. Therefore, the prevailing handling of neural signals in DANNs could lead to redundant representation as any neural signal could contain some partial information from other neural signals. To tackle that challenge, we suggest to employ the data-driven generalization of PCE theory known as arbitrary polynomial chaos (aPC) to construct a corresponding multi-variate orthonormal representations on each node of a DANN to obtain Deep arbitrary polynomial chaos neural networks.

paper_metadata.title: Learning Active Subspaces and Discovering Important Features with Gaussian Radial Basis Functions Neural Networks
paper_metadata.abstract: Providing a model that achieves a strong predictive performance and is simultaneously interpretable by humans is one of the most difficult challenges in machine learning research due to the conflicting nature of these two objectives. To address this challenge, we propose a modification of the radial basis function neural network model by equipping its Gaussian kernel with a learnable precision matrix. We show that precious information is contained in the spectrum of the precision matrix that can be extracted once the training of the model is completed. In particular, the eigenvectors explain the directions of maximum sensitivity of the model revealing the active subspace and suggesting potential applications for supervised dimensionality reduction. At the same time, the eigenvectors highlight the relationship in terms of absolute variation between the input and the latent variables, thereby allowing us to extract a ranking of the input variables based on their importance to the prediction task enhancing the model interpretability. We conducted numerical experiments for regression, classification, and feature selection tasks, comparing our model against popular machine learning models, the state-of-the-art deep learning-based embedding feature selection techniques, and a transformer model for tabular data. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model does not only yield an attractive prediction performance compared to the competitors but also provides meaningful and interpretable results that potentially could assist the decision-making process in real-world applications. A PyTorch implementation of the model is available on GitHub at the following link. https://github.com/dannyzx/Gaussian-RBFNN

paper_metadata.title: Learning Constrained Dynamics with Gauss Principle adhering Gaussian Processes
paper_metadata.abstract: The identification of the constrained dynamics of mechanical systems is often challenging. Learning methods promise to ease an analytical analysis, but require considerable amounts of data for training. We propose to combine insights from analytical mechanics with Gaussian process regression to improve the model's data efficiency and constraint integrity. The result is a Gaussian process model that incorporates a priori constraint knowledge such that its predictions adhere to Gauss' principle of least constraint. In return, predictions of the system's acceleration naturally respect potentially non-ideal (non-)holonomic equality constraints. As corollary results, our model enables to infer the acceleration of the unconstrained system from data of the constrained system and enables knowledge transfer between differing constraint configurations.

paper_metadata.title: A Parametric and Feasibility Study for Data Sampling of the Dynamic Mode Decomposition--Range, Resolution, and Universal Convergence States
paper_metadata.abstract: Scientific research and engineering practice often require the modeling and decomposition of nonlinear systems. The Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) is a novel Koopman-based technique that effectively dissects high-dimensional nonlinear systems into periodically distinct constituents on reduced-order subspaces. As a novel mathematical hatchling, the DMD bears vast potentials yet an equal degree of unknown. This serial effort investigates the nuances of DMD sampling with an engineering-oriented emphasis. This Part I aimed at elucidating how sampling range and resolution affect the convergence of DMD modes. We employed the most classical nonlinear system in fluid mechanics as the test subject--the turbulent free-shear flow over a prism--for optimal pertinency. We numerically simulated the flow by the dynamic-stress Large-Eddies Simulation with Near-Wall Resolution. With the large-quantity, high-fidelity data, we parametrized and identified four global convergence states: Initialization, Transition, Stabilization, and Divergence with increasing sampling range. Results showed that the Stabilization is the optimal state for modal convergence, in which DMD output becomes independent of the sampling range. The Initialization state also yields sufficient accuracy for most system reconstruction tasks. Moreover, defying popular beliefs, over-sampling causes algorithmic instability: as the temporal dimension, n, approaches and transcends the spatial dimension, m (i.e., m < n), the output diverges and becomes meaningless. Additionally, the convergence of the sampling resolution depends on the mode-specific dynamics, such that the resolution of 15 frames per cycle for target activities is suggested for most engineering implementations. Finally, a bi-parametric study revealed that the convergence of the sampling range and resolution are mutually independent.

paper_metadata.title: A Tutorial about Random Neural Networks in Supervised Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Random Neural Networks (RNNs) are a class of Neural Networks (NNs) that can also be seen as a specific type of queuing network. They have been successfully used in several domains during the last 25 years, as queuing networks to analyze the performance of resource sharing in many engineering areas, as learning tools and in combinatorial optimization, where they are seen as neural systems, and also as models of neurological aspects of living beings. In this article we focus on their learning capabilities, and more specifically, we present a practical guide for using the RNN to solve supervised learning problems. We give a general description of these models using almost indistinctly the terminology of Queuing Theory and the neural one. We present the standard learning procedures used by RNNs, adapted from similar well-established improvements in the standard NN field. We describe in particular a set of learning algorithms covering techniques based on the use of first order and, then, of second order derivatives. We also discuss some issues related to these objects and present new perspectives about their use in supervised learning problems. The tutorial describes their most relevant applications, and also provides a large bibliography.

paper_metadata.title: Strengthening the Training of Convolutional Neural Networks By Using Walsh Matrix
paper_metadata.abstract: DNN structures are continuously developing and achieving high performances in classification problems. Also, it is observed that success rates obtained with DNNs are higher than those obtained with traditional neural networks. In addition, one of the advantages of DNNs is that there is no need to spend an extra effort to determine the features; the CNN automatically extracts the features from the dataset during the training. Besides their benefits, the DNNs have the following three major drawbacks among the others: (i) Researchers have struggled with over-fitting and under-fitting issues in the training of DNNs, (ii) determination of even a coarse structure for the DNN may take days, and (iii) most of the time, the proposed network structure is too large to be too bulky to be used in real time applications. We have modified the training and structure of DNN to increase the classification performance, to decrease the number of nodes in the structure, and to be used with less number of hyper parameters. A minimum distance network (MDN) following the last layer of the convolutional neural network (CNN) is used as the classifier instead of a fully connected neural network (FCNN). In order to strengthen the training of the CNN, we suggest employing Walsh function. We tested the performances of the proposed DNN (named as DivFE) on the classification of ECG, EEG, heart sound, detection pneumonia in X-ray chest images, detection of BGA solder defects, and patterns of benchmark datasets (MNIST, IRIS, CIFAR10 and CIFAR20). In different areas, it has been observed that a higher classification performance was obtained by using the DivFE with less number of nodes.

paper_metadata.title: Continual Learning for Recurrent Neural Networks: an Empirical Evaluation
paper_metadata.abstract: Learning continuously during all model lifetime is fundamental to deploy machine learning solutions robust to drifts in the data distribution. Advances in Continual Learning (CL) with recurrent neural networks could pave the way to a large number of applications where incoming data is non stationary, like natural language processing and robotics. However, the existing body of work on the topic is still fragmented, with approaches which are application-specific and whose assessment is based on heterogeneous learning protocols and datasets. In this paper, we organize the literature on CL for sequential data processing by providing a categorization of the contributions and a review of the benchmarks. We propose two new benchmarks for CL with sequential data based on existing datasets, whose characteristics resemble real-world applications. We also provide a broad empirical evaluation of CL and Recurrent Neural Networks in class-incremental scenario, by testing their ability to mitigate forgetting with a number of different strategies which are not specific to sequential data processing. Our results highlight the key role played by the sequence length and the importance of a clear specification of the CL scenario.

paper_metadata.title: Optimal hierarchical modular topologies for producing limited sustained activation of neural networks
paper_metadata.abstract: An essential requirement for the representation of functional patterns in complex neural networks, such as the mammalian cerebral cortex, is the existence of stable regimes of network activation, typically arising from a limited parameter range. In this range of limited sustained activity (LSA), the activity of neural populations in the network persists between the extremes of either quickly dying out or activating the whole network. Hierarchical modular networks were previously found to show a wider parameter range for LSA than random or small-world networks not possessing hierarchical organization or multiple modules. Here we explored how variation in the number of hierarchical levels and modules per level influenced network dynamics and occurrence of LSA. We tested hierarchical configurations of different network sizes, approximating the large-scale networks linking cortical columns in one hemisphere of the rat, cat, or macaque monkey brain. Scaling of the network size affected the number of hierarchical levels and modules in the optimal networks, also depending on whether global edge density or the numbers of connections per node were kept constant. For constant edge density, only few network configurations, possessing an intermediate number of levels and a large number of modules, led to a large range of LSA independent of brain size. For a constant number of node connections, there was a trend for optimal configurations in larger-size networks to possess a larger number of hierarchical levels or more modules. These results may help to explain the trend to greater network complexity apparent in larger brains and may indicate that this complexity is required for maintaining stable levels of neural activation.

rag_package.related_work_summary: While deep neural networks are often studied for their generalization within distribution (Oladyshkin et al., 2023), their ability to extrapolate and achieve infinite generalization beyond the training data, as seen in algorithm development, remains a critical area of investigation. Addressing the question of how neural networks generalize from sufficient finite training experience (Basterrech and Rubino, 2016; lmez and Dokur, 2021), this work focuses on the learning dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequential tasks. Prior research has explored learning dynamics for RNNs in various contexts, such as continual learning to mitigate forgetting in non-stationary data (Cossu et al., 2021), or incorporating prior knowledge into learning models to improve data efficiency (Geist and Trimpe, 2020). The concept of learned algorithms leading to robust generalization is also related to understanding model interpretability, where neural networks might learn to abstract or simplify data representations for improved predictive power (D'Agostino et al., 2023). However, the specific mechanism of an 'implicit representational merger effect' leading to finite automaton construction for infinite generalization is less explored, differentiating it from analyses of network stability and limited sustained activation (Kaiser and Hilgetag, 2010), or discussions on general data sampling effects (Li et al., 2021).

reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly exciting and novel perspective on infinite generalization in neural networks, a phenomenon that has long challenged our understanding. The core idea of 'implicit state merger' driven by gradient descent, leading to the formation of a finite automaton, is a significant intellectual leap. While the theoretical derivations are complex and could benefit from further distillation, the intuition behind the two-phase algorithm development – initial tree fitting followed by representational merging – offers a powerful explanatory framework. The authors thoughtfully connect this to related phenomena like 'rich and lazy learning' and even discuss implications for neuroscience. The findings, particularly the phase transition to perfect generalization and the explanation for redundant states, push the boundaries of interpretability and provide a foundation for future inquiries into how neural networks learn real algorithms. Despite some minor imperfections in clarity or evaluation generalizability to all possible architectures, the bold theoretical contribution and its potential impact on understanding deep learning's algorithmic capabilities make this paper a strong candidate for acceptance.

4.desc: No RAG, 3 iterations, 1 reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper introduces a compelling and innovative theoretical framework to explain infinite generalization in RNNs, focusing on an 'implicit state merger' effect that leads to the formation of finite automata. This is a bold attempt to provide effective theories for complex neural network behaviors.

The concept of algorithm development occurring in two distinct phases (tree-fitting then generalization via state merger) is a novel and insightful contribution, offering a new perspective on how NN's transition from memorization to genuine algorithmic understanding. This phase transition idea is particularly exciting.

The paper connects low-level representational dynamics to high-level algorithmic behavior (DFA formation), providing a mechanistic explanation for a phenomenon that often seems mysterious. This interpretability aspect is highly significant for understanding deep learning's capabilities.
weaknesses: While the theoretical model offers significant insights, it abstracts away many real-world complexities (e.g., specific architectural inductive biases, regularization, noise). The authors acknowledge this, but it implies a need for further work to bridge the gap between this effective theory and the full complexity of real-world deep learning systems.

The evaluation, while illustrative and appropriately focused for a theoretical paper, primarily relies on synthetic tasks. While the authors justify this choice for clarity, a broader empirical validation across different types of algorithmic tasks would strengthen the generalizability claims.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a highly novel and significant contribution to understanding the 'infinite generalization' phenomenon in neural networks. The central idea of implicit representational merger leading to finite automaton construction is ingenious and provides a clear, mechanistic explanation for how RNNs can learn true algorithms. I am particularly excited by the two-phase development theory and the connection between representational dynamics and algorithmic emergence. The authors' rebuttal successfully clarifies and reinforces their position regarding the intentional abstraction of their model and the choice of synthetic tasks, emphasizing their goal of identifying a fundamental mechanism in a clear setting. I concur that establishing these foundational principles is a crucial first step for future comprehensive work. The work's potential impact on interpretability and neuroscience remains extremely high. This paper is a significant and bold step forward in understanding deep learning's capabilities, making it an enthusiastic 'Accept'.

why_it_fits: The paper directly addresses 'general machine learning' with a focus on 'deep learning (theory, etc.)' and 'reinforcement learning (decision and control)' in the context of sequence processing, which is a core and central topic for ICML.

The contribution involves a novel theoretical framework and an 'effective theory for the representational dynamics' in RNNs, which aligns well with ICML's interest in theory of machine learning and deep learning theory.

The paper offers a mechanistic explanation for infinite generalization, connecting low-level representational dynamics to high-level algorithmic behavior, which is a significant aspect of 'trustworthy machine learning (interpretability)' and understanding general machine learning phenomena.

Reviewer A acknowledges the 'compelling and innovative theoretical framework' and 'novel and insightful contribution' regarding the two-phase development, indicating a strong novelty fit for ICML, which values cutting-edge research.
why_it_does_not_fit: While the theoretical foundation is strong, the evaluation primarily uses synthetic tasks ('streaming parity task', 'random regular tasks') rather than large-scale, complex real-world applications. Reviewer A notes that 'a broader empirical validation across different types of algorithmic tasks would strengthen the generalizability claims,' which might be a minor detractor for some ICML reviewers looking for immediate real-world impact.

The explicit abstraction acknowledged by the authors ('abstracts away many real-world complexities (e.g., specific architectural inductive biases, regularization, noise)'), though justified for theoretical clarity, could be seen as a limitation by reviewers expecting models closer to practical application.

why_it_fits: The paper specifically studies the learning dynamics of 'recurrent neural networks (RNNs)' and 'deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.)', which are central to ICLR's focus.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel and insightful 'implicit representational merger effect' to explain infinite generalization in RNNs, which is a significant departure from typical interpolation-focused generalization theories.
The use of a simplified interaction model, abstracting away architectural details, is a bold and creative approach to uncover universal mechanisms underlying algorithm development in deep networks.

The identification of two distinct phases in algorithm development (tree fitting and generalization via merging) provides a compelling and interpretable narrative for how complex computational abilities can emerge from simple gradient descent.
The study bridges concepts between deep learning and neuroscience, offering a new perspective on algorithm development that could inspire future research in both fields.
weaknesses: While the simplified interaction model is conceptually powerful, its direct applicability to the full complexity of real-world neural networks might be limited, and the transition from abstract dynamics to concrete architectural implications could be stronger.

The evaluation, while providing empirical evidence for the proposed phases and the interaction model's predictions, relies heavily on a single task (streaming parity) and randomly generated automata. More diverse and complex tasks with varying levels of algorithmic structure would strengthen the claims about universality.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly exciting and innovative perspective on how deep neural networks can achieve infinite generalization by learning actual algorithms. The concept of implicit representational merger and the two-phase algorithm development narrative are highly novel and offer profound insights into the inductive biases of gradient descent. While the theoretical model is simplified and the empirical validation focuses on relatively constrained tasks, the core idea is so compelling and potentially transformative that it warrants acceptance. Minor methodological approximations are acceptable given the groundbreaking nature of the proposed mechanism. This work pushes the boundaries of our understanding of generalization and algorithmic learning in AI, and its implications for both machine learning and neuroscience are substantial.

strengths: The paper rigorously develops a local interaction theory for representational learning dynamics in RNNs, which accurately predicts the observed two-phase algorithm development (tree fitting and state merger). The mathematical derivations in the appendix are detailed and thorough.

The core idea of interpreting RNN behavior through the lens of Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) and explicitly extracting these automata with a well-defined state reduction algorithm provides a highly precise and interpretable method for analyzing learning dynamics and generalization.

The formulation of the 'implicit state merger' condition, stemming from continuity and gradient descent dynamics (Equation 7), offers a compelling and mathematically grounded explanation for how finite generalization can transition to infinite generalization with sufficient training and appropriate conditions.
weaknesses: While the theoretical models capture key aspects, the paper acknowledges limitations regarding higher-order/global interactions and inductive biases from architectural choices. The extent to which these disregarded factors might alter the observed dynamics or condition the 'universality' of the findings remains somewhat underexplored.

The comparison with Transformers in Section 6.3 is qualitative and highlights differences (e.g., hidden states not merging, but attention matrices showing patterns). A more rigorous theoretical extension or a detailed discussion on why the current interaction model might not fully apply to Transformers would strengthen this section.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a strong theoretical and empirical investigation into the phenomenon of infinite generalization in RNNs, particularly focusing on the streaming parity task. The core contribution is a robust mathematical model explaining how representational states merge during training, leading to the formation of a finite automaton and thus perfect generalization. The methodological approach of extracting and analyzing DFAs is sound, providing clear insights into the learning dynamics. The explanation of the two-phase development (tree fitting followed by state merger) and the derivation of conditions for merger are particularly compelling. While some limitations regarding the scope of the theoretical model and the less direct applicability to Transformers exist, the rigor in the analysis of RNNs on this task is commendable and advances our understanding of generalization beyond interpolation.

strengths: The paper tackles a highly significant practical problem: understanding how deep neural networks generalize, especially out-of-distribution (infinite generalization). This is crucial for building reliable and trustworthy AI systems.

The use of the streaming parity task as a case study is well-chosen. Its simplicity allows for detailed theoretical analysis while still exhibiting complex generalization behavior observed in larger models. This makes the insights potentially transferable.

The proposed 'implicit state merger' theory, derived from a local interaction model of representational dynamics, offers a clear and interpretable mechanism for understanding algorithm development and generalization. This provides concrete insights for practitioners.

The demonstration of a phase transition from interpolation to infinite generalization, along with the explanation for the initial 'tree fitting' phase and the concept of 'redundant states,' adds considerable depth to our understanding of learning dynamics.
weaknesses: While the theoretical model (local interaction, smooth expressive maps) is useful for gaining intuition, the discussion on its limitations (e.g., ignoring higher-order interactions, architectural biases, regularization, noise, and shared parameters) should be more prominent. Practitioners considering these insights for real-world systems need to be acutely aware of where this simplified model might break down.

The application to Transformers (Section 6.3) is somewhat brief and acknowledges that the DFA interpretation is less straightforward. While it's good to mention, the lack of a clear, analogous mechanism for transformers weakens the claim of broader applicability and leaves a question mark for practitioners heavily using transformers.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a compelling theoretical framework to explain how recurrent neural networks can achieve 'infinite generalization' on algorithmic tasks. The chosen streaming parity task serves as an excellent case study, allowing the authors to develop an interpretable theory grounded in representational dynamics and state mergers. The concept of implicit state mergers, the observed phase transitions in learning, and the explanation of redundant states are highly significant for practitioners seeking to understand and build more robust AI models. While the theoretical model simplifies some aspects of neural network training, the insights gained are valuable and clearly communicated. The paper's focus on practical relevance and the mechanistic understanding of how algorithms emerge in NNs makes it a strong contribution to the field. The identified limitations are acknowledged, but a slightly more thorough discussion of when the simplified theoretical model might not hold would further enhance its practical utility.

why_it_fits: The paper's topic of understanding generalization, particularly 'infinite generalization' and algorithm development in neural networks, aligns well with ICML's focus on general machine learning, deep learning theory, and trustworthy machine learning (reliability, robustness, safety).

This kind of theoretical and mechanistic understanding of deep learning is highly valued at ICML, as highlighted by Reviewers A and B.

The paper's exploration of recurrent dynamics, interpretation of RNNs as finite automata, and the explanation of how these automata are formed during training is highly relevant to topics such as graph learning, theoretical machine learning, and general machine learning.

The paper makes connections to neuroscience, suggesting that findings could inspire research in both fields, fitting within 'application-driven machine learning' categories that touch on biological or cognitive inspiration.
why_it_does_not_fit: While the paper's theoretical model is insightful, its direct applicability to the full complexity of real-world neural networks and more diverse, complex tasks is acknowledged as a limitation by all reviewers. The section on Transformers (6.3) is briefly discussed and acknowledges that the insights are less straightforwardly applicable, potentially making the work less appealing to segments of the ICML audience heavily focused on transformer architectures.

why_it_fits: The paper directly addresses 'General machine learning: core contributions in supervised and unsupervised methods' by exploring fundamental generalization mechanisms in RNNs, which is a key focus for NeurIPS.

strengths: The paper introduces EMBODIEDBENCH, a comprehensive and truly novel benchmark that addresses a significant gap in evaluating MLLM-based embodied agents. The inclusion of diverse action levels (high-level and low-level) and fine-grained, capability-oriented subsets is a much-needed innovation, going beyond previous benchmarks' limitations.

The findings are highly significant and provide crucial insights for the field. Identifying that MLLMs excel at high-level tasks but struggle with low-level manipulation, and that long-horizon planning is a major bottleneck, directly informs future research directions and model development.

The evaluation is extensive, testing 24 leading MLLMs (both proprietary and open-source) across the proposed benchmark. This broad empirical analysis establishes a clear baseline and demonstrates the utility of EMBODIEDBENCH.

The ablation studies, particularly those on the role of vision, image resolution, and visual in-context learning, provide practical and actionable insights for designing more effective MLLM-based embodied agents.
weaknesses: The soundess could be improved in terms of clarity regarding the discretization of the action space for EB-Manipulation. For example, how 'Roll', 'Pitch', 'Yaw' (Euler angles) map to 0-120 bins without losing critical continuous information for fine motor control is not fully elaborated.

While the paper acknowledges the limitation of simulated environments, the absence of discussion on sim-to-real transfer challenges, even conceptually, could be seen as a minor oversight for a paper focusing on 'real-world tasks' in its abstract.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a highly novel and significant contribution to the field of embodied AI. EMBODIEDBENCH is a critical step forward in evaluating MLLM-based agents, filling a crucial gap by offering a diverse, hierarchical, and capability-focused benchmark. The findings are not only eye-opening, revealing clear strengths and weaknesses of current models, but also provide actionable insights for future research. While there are minor points regarding the detail of action space discretization, these do not detract from the overall bold vision and potential impact of this work. The paper is well-structured and clear, making it an excellent resource for researchers. I strongly recommend acceptance.

why_it_fits: The paper introduces a comprehensive benchmarking suite, EMBODIEDBENCH, for Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in vision-driven embodied agents. why_it_fits: The paper heavily involves 'deep learning' and 'Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs)', which are central to ICLR's focus. The evaluation of '24 leading proprietary and open-source MLLMs' is highly relevant.

why_it_does_not_fit: While deep learning is at its core, the paper's primary contribution is a benchmark rather than proposing a novel deep learning model, optimization technique, or theoretical insight into deep learning itself. strengths: The paper introduces EMBODIEDBENCH, a comprehensive and truly novel benchmark that addresses a significant gap in the evaluation of MLLM-based embodied agents. Its dual focus on diverse action levels (high-level to low-level manipulation) and fine-grained, capability-oriented subsets is a substantial advancement over existing benchmarks.

The thorough experimental evaluation of 24 leading MLLMs (both proprietary and open-source) provides invaluable insights into the current state of the art. The findings, particularly the struggle of MLLMs with low-level manipulation and long-horizon planning, are critical for guiding future research directions.

The proposed unified agent framework, designed to maximize the potential of off-the-shelf MLLMs for both high and low-level tasks, is a practical and well-thought-out component of the benchmark. This framework itself contributes to advancing how MLLMs can be deployed in embodied settings.
weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges the limitation of being solely in simulation, the lack of discussion or clear pathways for bridging the sim-to-real gap, beyond general statements, slightly diminishes the long-term impact in practical applications. More concrete ideas on how the benchmark findings might translate or guide real-world robot deployment would be beneficial.

The ablation studies provide good insights, but some details could be expanded. For instance, the observation that "current MLLMs struggle to understand multiple historical images effectively" is mentioned without much mechanistic exploration or proposed solutions, leaving a key challenge somewhat underexplored in terms of understanding *why* it struggles.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents EMBODIEDBENCH, a highly novel and significant contribution to the field of embodied AI. The benchmark's comprehensive design, covering both hierarchical action levels and fine-grained capabilities across multiple environments, is a clear step forward. The extensive evaluation of 24 MLLMs and the derived insights regarding current limitations (e.g., low-level manipulation, long-horizon planning) are incredibly valuable for researchers. While the reliance on simulation and some unaddressed 'why' questions in ablations are minor concerns, the overall ambition, innovative approach, and the potential to accelerate research in MLLM-based embodied agents are exceptionally strong. I am particularly impressed by the creation of new datasets and enhancements to existing simulators to support this multifaceted evaluation. This is exactly the kind of bold, forward-thinking work that pushes the boundaries of the field.

target_paper_summary.title: Ebench : Comprehensive Benchmarking Multi-Modal Large Language Models For Vision-Driven Embodied Agents
target_paper_summary.abstract: Leveraging Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to create embodied agents offers a promising avenue for tackling real-world tasks. While language-centric embodied agents have garnered substantial attention, MLLM-based embodied agents remain underexplored due to the lack of comprehensive evaluation frameworks. To bridge this gap, we introduce EMBODIEDBENCH, an extensive benchmark designed to evaluate visiondriven embodied agents. EMBODIEDBENCH features: (1) a diverse set of 1,128 testing tasks across four environments, ranging from high-level semantic tasks (e.g., household) to low-level tasks involving atomic actions (e.g., navigation and manipulation); and (2) six meticulously curated subsets evaluating essential agent capabilities like commonsense reasoning, complex instruction understanding, spatial awareness, visual perception, and long-term planning. Through extensive experiments, we evaluated 24 leading proprietary and open-source MLLMs within EMBODIEDBENCH. Our findings reveal that: MLLMs excel at highlevel tasks but struggle with low-level manipulation, with the best model, GPT-4o, scoring only 28.9% on average. EMBODIEDBENCH provides a multifaceted standardized evaluation platform that not only highlights existing challenges but also offers valuable insights to advance MLLM- based embodied agents. Our code and dataset are available at https://embodiedbench.github.io.

paper_metadata.title: Developing Embodied Multisensory Dialogue Agents
paper_metadata.abstract: A few decades of work in the AI field have focused efforts on developing a new generation of systems which can acquire knowledge via interaction with the world. Yet, until very recently, most such attempts were underpinned by research which predominantly regarded linguistic phenomena as separated from the brain and body. This could lead one into believing that to emulate linguistic behaviour, it suffices to develop 'software' operating on abstract representations that will work on any computational machine. This picture is inaccurate for several reasons, which are elucidated in this paper and extend beyond sensorimotor and semantic resonance. Beginning with a review of research, I list several heterogeneous arguments against disembodied language, in an attempt to draw conclusions for developing embodied multisensory agents which communicate verbally and non-verbally with their environment. Without taking into account both the architecture of the human brain, and embodiment, it is unrealistic to replicate accurately the processes which take place during language acquisition, comprehension, production, or during non-linguistic actions. While robots are far from isomorphic with humans, they could benefit from strengthened associative connections in the optimization of their processes and their reactivity and sensitivity to environmental stimuli, and in situated human-machine interaction. The concept of multisensory integration should be extended to cover linguistic input and the complementary information combined from temporally coincident sensory impressions.

paper_metadata.title: EmbodiedCity: A Benchmark Platform for Embodied Agent in Real-world City Environment
paper_metadata.abstract: Embodied artificial intelligence emphasizes the role of an agent's body in generating human-like behaviors. The recent efforts on EmbodiedAI pay a lot of attention to building up machine learning models to possess perceiving, planning, and acting abilities, thereby enabling real-time interaction with the world. However, most works focus on bounded indoor environments, such as navigation in a room or manipulating a device, with limited exploration of embodying the agents in open-world scenarios. That is, embodied intelligence in the open and outdoor environment is less explored, for which one potential reason is the lack of high-quality simulators, benchmarks, and datasets. To address it, in this paper, we construct a benchmark platform for embodied intelligence evaluation in real-world city environments. Specifically, we first construct a highly realistic 3D simulation environment based on the real buildings, roads, and other elements in a real city. In this environment, we combine historically collected data and simulation algorithms to conduct simulations of pedestrian and vehicle flows with high fidelity. Further, we designed a set of evaluation tasks covering different EmbodiedAI abilities. Moreover, we provide a complete set of input and output interfaces for access, enabling embodied agents to easily take task requirements and current environmental observations as input and then make decisions and obtain performance evaluations. On the one hand, it expands the capability of existing embodied intelligence to higher levels. On the other hand, it has a higher practical value in the real world and can support more potential applications for artificial general intelligence. Based on this platform, we evaluate some popular large language models for embodied intelligence capabilities of different dimensions and difficulties.

paper_metadata.title: TEAL: Tokenize and Embed ALL for Multi-modal Large Language Models
paper_metadata.abstract: Despite Multi-modal Large Language Models (MM-LLMs) have made exciting strides recently, they are still struggling to efficiently model the interactions among multi-modal inputs and the generation in non-textual modalities. In this work, we propose TEAL (Tokenize and Embed ALl)}, an approach to treat the input from any modality as a token sequence and learn a joint embedding space for all modalities. Specifically, for the input from any modality, TEAL first discretizes it into a token sequence with the off-the-shelf tokenizer and embeds the token sequence into a joint embedding space with a learnable embedding matrix. MM-LLMs just need to predict the multi-modal tokens autoregressively as the textual LLMs do. Finally, the corresponding de-tokenizer is applied to generate the output in each modality based on the predicted token sequence. With the joint embedding space, TEAL enables the frozen LLMs to perform both understanding and generation tasks involving non-textual modalities, such as image and audio. Thus, the textual LLM can just work as an interface and maintain its high performance in textual understanding and generation. Experiments show that TEAL achieves substantial improvements in multi-modal understanding, and implements a simple scheme for multi-modal generations.

paper_metadata.title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
paper_metadata.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved success in acting as agents, which interact with environments through tools such as search engines. However, LLMs are optimized for language generation instead of tool use during training or alignment, limiting their effectiveness as agents. To resolve this problem, previous work has first collected interaction trajectories between LLMs and environments, using only trajectories that successfully finished the task to fine-tune smaller models, making fine-tuning data scarce and acquiring it both difficult and costly. Discarding failed trajectories also leads to significant wastage of data and resources and limits the possible optimization paths during fine-tuning. In this paper, we argue that unsuccessful trajectories offer valuable insights, and LLMs can learn from these trajectories through appropriate quality control and fine-tuning strategies. By simply adding a prefix or suffix that tells the model whether to generate a successful trajectory during training, we improve model performance by a large margin on mathematical reasoning, multi-hop question answering, and strategic question answering tasks. We further analyze the inference results and find that our method provides a better trade-off between valuable information and errors in unsuccessful trajectories. To our knowledge, we are the first to demonstrate the value of negative trajectories and their application in agent-tunning scenarios. Our findings offer guidance for developing better agent-tuning methods and low-resource data usage techniques.

strengths: The core idea of a comprehensive, capability-oriented benchmark for MLLM-based embodied agents, covering both high-level and low-level tasks, is highly novel and timely. This directly addresses a critical gap in the field.

weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges the simulation-only nature as a limitation, the lack of real-world validation inevitably raises questions about the generalizability of some findings, especially for low-level tasks that demand high fidelity.

reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly exciting and significant contribution to the field of embodied AI. The core novelty lies in its comprehensive, hierarchical, and capability-oriented benchmark (EMBODIEDBENCH) for MLLM-based embodied agents. This is precisely the kind of bold, innovative work that pushes the boundaries. The dual focus on high-level semantic tasks and low-level atomic actions, combined with a fine-grained evaluation of critical agent capabilities, is a major step beyond existing benchmarks. The extensive evaluation results and ablation studies offer invaluable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of current MLLMs, clearly outlining future research directions. While the simulation-only nature is a common limitation in this domain, it doesn't detract from the profound impact this benchmark will have on guiding the development of more capable embodied agents. The insights on MLLM struggles with low-level manipulation and long-horizon planning, and the critical role of vision in low-level tasks, are particularly noteworthy. This work is highly significant and deserves to be recognized.

strengths: The paper introduces EMBODIEDBENCH, a comprehensive and meticulously designed benchmark that addresses a significant gap in the evaluation of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for embodied agents. Its dual focus on diverse task action levels (high-level and low-level) and fine-grained, capability-oriented evaluation (six distinct capabilities) is a strong point, providing a more holistic assessment than previous benchmarks.

The experimental design is exceptionally rigorous, evaluating 24 leading MLLMs (both proprietary and open-source) across 1,128 testing tasks. This extensive empirical validation, coupled with detailed ablation studies on critical factors like vision input, resolution, detection boxes, and visual in-context learning, provides rich insights and robust findings.

The detailed error analysis of GPT-4o in both high-level (EB-ALFRED) and low-level (EB-Manipulation) tasks is highly valuable. Breaking down failures into perception, reasoning, and planning errors, and further categorizing sub-errors, offers concrete directions for future model development and highlights specific areas where current MLLMs struggle.
weaknesses: While the paper justifies the use of simulated environments for reproducibility and cost-effectiveness, the absence of any discussion or preliminary steps towards bridging the simulation-to-reality gap is a moderate weakness. Given the inherent challenges in transferring policies from simulation to physical robots, acknowledging this more directly could strengthen the paper's scope for real-world impact.

The agent design, while unified and robust for evaluation, seems somewhat decoupled from the inherent capabilities of MLLMs. The paper mentions discretizing action spaces and adding detection boxes to "overcome this challenge" for MLLMs in low-level manipulation. A deeper exploration or discussion on how these pre-processing/post-processing steps might constrain or bias the MLLMs' true potential, or how they could be integrated more organically, would be beneficial.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents EMBODIEDBENCH, a highly valuable and well-executed benchmark for multi-modal large language models in embodied AI. The comprehensive nature of the benchmark, covering both high-level and low-level tasks, and providing fine-grained capability-oriented evaluation, is a significant contribution. The evaluation is thorough, including a large array of models and insightful ablation studies. The findings are clearly presented and provide practical implications for future research. While the reliance on simulated environments is a common trade-off, a more explicit discussion of sim-to-real transfer could be beneficial. Overall, the methodological rigor and the depth of analysis make this a strong contribution to the field.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly significant and timely problem: the comprehensive evaluation of MLLM-based embodied agents. The lack of standardized, multi-faceted benchmarks has been a hindrance to progress in this area, and EMBODIEDBENCH fills this gap admirably.

The benchmark is exceptionally comprehensive, incorporating diverse task environments (high-level household, low-level navigation and manipulation) and meticulously designed capability-oriented subsets (commonsense, complex instruction, spatial awareness, visual perception, long-horizon planning). This fine-grained evaluation offers deep insights beyond simple task success.

The experimental evaluation is extensive, comparing 24 leading MLLMs (both proprietary and open-source). The findings, such as the clear distinction in performance between high-level and low-level tasks, the challenge of long-horizon planning, and the critical role of vision in low-level tasks, provide invaluable practical insights for practitioners and researchers directly involved in building these agents.
weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges the limitation of relying solely on simulated environments, it's a critical point for a 'practical impact' persona. The sim-to-real gap is substantial in embodied AI, and even the most comprehensive simulated benchmark might not fully reflect real-world performance challenges.

The agent framework, while unified, relies on a pre-defined set of 'skills' or action primitives, especially for high-level tasks. This limits the assessment of an MLLM's ability to truly 'reason' about novel actions or dynamically compose skills not explicitly provided. The discretization of low-level actions, while pragmatic, also abstracts away some of the continuous control challenges.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper introduces EMBODIEDBENCH, a much-needed and highly comprehensive benchmark for evaluating Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as embodied agents. target_paper_summary.title: Rlef: Grounding Code Llms In Execution Feedback With Reinforcement Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as agents solve user-specified tasks over multiple steps while keeping the required manual engagement to a minimum. Crucially, such LLMs need to ground their generations in any feedback obtained to reliably achieve the desired outcomes. We propose an end-to-end reinforcement learning method for teaching models to leverage execution feedback in the realm of code synthesis, where state-of-the-art LLMs struggle to improve code iteratively compared to independent sampling. We benchmark on competitive programming tasks and achieve large performance gains with both small (8B parameters) and large (70B) models, outperforming previous work while reducing the number of samples required by an order of magnitude. Our analysis of inference-time behavior demonstrates that our method produces LLMs that effectively leverage automatic feedback over multiple steps.

paper_metadata.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
paper_metadata.abstract: I created a basic proof of concept of LMVM (Language Model Virtual Machine), a command line toolchain that English instructions into native binaries without intermediary high-level language compilation. The command line uses a large language model (LLM) as IR generation backend, producing LLVM Intermediate Representation (IR) directly from user instructions coding. The IR is compiled and linked to machine code (-o files) via `clang` (with an `llc`/`lld` fallback on POSIX hosts) and executed on bare metal, within Docker sandboxes, on AWS Lambda, or as standalone HTTP servers. How It Works (5 Steps) 1. You type an instruction - e.g. "Create a rest api running on localhost port 3000 and return hello world" 2. LMVM checks your computer - It figures out if you're on Windows/Mac/Linux, what CPU you have (Intel vs ARM), and makes sure clang (the compiler) is installed. If not, it offers to install it for you (with your permission). 3. An AI writes LLVM IR - Instead of writing C or Python, the LLM writes LLVM IR -- a low-level assembly-like language that sits between source code and machine code. The prompt includes your OS details so the AI generates code that works on your platform (e.g. Winsock on Windows vs POSIX sockets on Mac/Linux). 4. Clang turns IR into a native binary - clang compiles the IR and links it with system libraries (PostgreSQL, OpenSSL, SQLite, etc.) into a real executable. One step, no extra tools needed. 5. It runs - The binary executes directly on your CPU. If it's a Docker target, it runs sandboxed. If it's Lambda, it packages for AWS. 2. Why we care : Compiled native binaries outperform interpreted languages by 10-50x in CPU usage and 5-15x in memory for compute-heavy tasks, because interpreters add overhead with every instruction they process and their single-threaded execution model blocks true parallelism. Few runtimes that compile code on the fly, the gap narrows to 2-5x in CPU since those systems optimize hot code paths over time -- but native code still starts faster, uses less memory, and can run true parallel threads instead of juggling everything through a single event loop. The biggest gains show up in recursive and number-crunching workloads (where the cost of "figuring out what to do next" dominates) and memory-heavy tasks (where automatic garbage collection and wrapping every value in an object bloats memory usage). I/O-bound tasks show the smallest differences, because the operating system does the real work regardless of what language runtime sits on top. This also means we need to think carefully about maintainability, especially now that AI agents can generate code as a complete black box sometimes even producing low-level output that humans rarely inspect. 3. System Architecture [CLI] → [Toolchain] → [LLM Client] → [Compiler] → [Runner] → Output ↑ | Error Feedback | Self‑Correction Loop (x10) 3.1 CLI and Interactive Setup The command-line interface (built on Commander.js) exposes four commands: `run` (compile and execute), `compile` (IR generation only), `build` (compile existing IR), and `targets` (list output targets). 3.2 LLM Client The LLM client wraps an OpenAI-compatible API, supporting providers examples (OpenAI, Groq, Together AI, OpenRouter, and local llm instances). The command line agent constructs prompts from two sources: a system prompt (loaded from `Prompt.md`, ~4000 tokens) containing LLVM IR generation rules, security constraints, and code templates; and a user prompt containing a platform descriptor (host OS, exact target triple, sockets dialect), the instruction, target, and error context for retry attempts. A secondary method, is used by the toolchain bootstrapper to obtain package-manager commands for the detected host. 3.3 Platform Abstraction and Toolchain Bootstrapper Since LMVM builds real native programs, it has to know exactly what computer it's running on -- the same code won't work the same way on Windows vs Mac vs Linux. So a platform module figures out three things: 1. The "target triple" -- a label that tells the compiler exactly which OS and CPU to build for (like x86_64-pc-windows-msvc for 64-bit Windows, or arm64-apple-darwin for an M-series Mac). 2. How to do networking -- Windows uses its own socket system (Winsock), while Mac and Linux use the standard POSIX approach. The code has to match. 3. What package manager is available -- winget/choco/scoop on Windows, brew on Mac, apt/dnf/pacman on Linux. This matters if LMVM needs to install something. All of this gets described in plain text and injected into the AI's prompt, so it writes code that actually compiles on your machine instead of assuming you're on Linux. Before talking to the AI, LMVM runs a checklist to make sure your computer can actually compile things: 1. PATH fix - If you just installed clang but your terminal hasn't refreshed yet, LMVM detects the install location and patches its own PATH so it finds clang right away, no need to restart your terminal. 2. Is clang there? - It checks that the compiler is actually available. 3. Can clang actually build a program? (Windows only) -- On Windows, having clang isn't enough -- it also needs the MSVC linker and Windows SDK behind it. LMVM compiles a tiny test program to verify the full chain works. If it fails, the Visual Studio Build Tools are probably missing. 4. Install with user's permission - If anything is missing, LMVM asks the AI for the right install commands, shows them to you, and waits for your yes before running anything. Then it checks again. If the toolchain still can't work after all that, LMVM stops early and tells you exactly what to do (install manually, open a new terminal, or use Docker instead). It doesn't waste your AI API calls retrying something a code fix can't solve. 3.4 Code Compiler Compilation is driven by `clang`, which lowers the `.ll` and invokes the platform linker in a single step: Primary path (all platforms) - `clang output.ll <lib-flags> -o <binary>`. Library flags are platform-aware: POSIX hosts use `-lpq`, `-lcurl`, `-lssl`, etc.; Windows links `ws2_32` for socket/server targets and relies on the MSVC C runtime. For the AWS Lambda target, static linking is applied. POSIX fallback - If `clang` is unavailable on macOS/Linux, the system falls back to the classic cascade: the LLVM Static Compiler (`llc -filetype=obj -relocation-model=pic`) to produce a position-independent object file, then `ld.lld` (`-flavor gnu`), the system C compiler (`cc`), or `clang` as a linker. A 60-second timeout bounds each invocation. The compiler maps library names to their respective linker flags through platform-specific lookup tables, covering PostgreSQL (libpq), HTTP (libcurl), JSON (cJSON), SSL/TLS (OpenSSL), image processing (libpng, libjpeg), databases (libsqlite3, libmysqlclient), compression (zlib), encryption (libcrypto), caching (hiredis), and message queues (librdkafka). 3.5 Execution Runner The runner dispatches binary execution based on the detected target like native , docker or AWS or GCR. 3.6 Self-Correction Loop When compilation or execution fails, the runtime updates a VM state object (`VMState`) with the error type (compiler/linker/runtime), error message, error line number, previous IR, and a compressed memory object (`VMMemory`) tracking accumulated errors and resolved dependencies. This enriched context is fed back to the LLM in the next attempt, enabling targeted correction. The loop terminates after a configurable maximum number of attempts (default: 10). 3.7 Security Layer LMVM employs defense-in-depth across three layers: 1. AI rules -- The instructions sent to the AI explicitly say: don't generate code that runs shell commands with user input, don't write files outside the allowed folder, don't read sensitive system files, don't hardcode passwords, and don't allocate unlimited memory. Think of this as a "don't do bad things" rulebook for the AI. 2. Sandbox -- When running in Docker, the program is locked down. A seccomp profile blocks the most dangerous system calls -- things like creating new processes, mounting drives, rebooting the machine, loading kernel modules, or snooping on other programs. Docker also limits the program to 512 MB of RAM and 1 CPU core, so it can't eat all your resources. This follows NIST security guidelines. 3. Input protection -- When LMVM runs the compiler or your program, it passes arguments as a structured list, not a single string. This means a hacker can't sneak in shell commands the way they might with string concatenation (the classic "shell injection" attack). The one exception is the toolchain installer, which does run shell commands -- but it always shows you the exact commands first and waits for your approval before running them. API keys are hidden in console output, and data buffers are capped at 10 MB to prevent memory explosions Appendix : As a demo using command LMVMcli command line we created a basic rest api directly as a machice code. paper_metadata.title: Harnessing the Power of LLMs in Practice: A Survey on ChatGPT and Beyond
paper_metadata.venue: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data
paper_metadata.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive and practical guide for practitioners and end-users working with Large Language Models (LLMs) in their downstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. We provide discussions and insights into the usage of LLMs from the perspectives of models, data, and downstream tasks. First, we offer an introduction and brief summary of current language models. Then, we discuss the influence of pre-training data, training data, and test data. Most importantly, we provide a detailed discussion about the use and non-use cases of large language models for various natural language processing tasks, such as knowledge-intensive tasks, traditional natural language understanding tasks, generation tasks, emergent abilities, and considerations for specific tasks. We present various use cases and non-use cases to illustrate the practical applications and limitations of LLMs in real-world scenarios. We also try to understand the importance of data and the specific challenges associated with each NLP task. Furthermore, we explore the impact of spurious biases on LLMs and delve into other essential considerations, such as efficiency, cost, and latency, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of deploying LLMs in practice. This comprehensive guide aims to provide researchers and practitioners with valuable insights and best practices for working with LLMs, thereby enabling the successful implementation of these models in a wide range of NLP tasks. A curated list of practical guide resources of LLMs, regularly updated, can be found at https://github.com/Mooler0410/LLMsPracticalGuide . An LLMs evolutionary tree, editable yet regularly updated, can be found at llmtree.ai .

paper_metadata.title: SoK: Hardware Defenses Against Speculative Execution Attacks
paper_metadata.abstract: Speculative execution attacks leverage the speculative and out-of-order execution features in modern computer processors to access secret data or execute code that should not be executed. Secret information can then be leaked through a covert channel. While software patches can be installed for mitigation on existing hardware, these solutions can incur big performance overhead. Hardware mitigation is being studied extensively by the computer architecture community. It has the benefit of preserving software compatibility and the potential for much smaller performance overhead than software solutions. This paper presents a systematization of the hardware defenses against speculative execution attacks that have been proposed. We show that speculative execution attacks consist of 6 critical attack steps. We propose defense strategies, each of which prevents a critical attack step from happening, thus preventing the attack from succeeding. We then summarize 20 hardware defenses and overhead-reducing features that have been proposed. We show that each defense proposed can be classified under one of our defense strategies, which also explains why it can thwart the attack from succeeding. We discuss the scope of the defenses, their performance overhead, and the security-performance trade-offs that can be made.

paper_metadata.title: Execution-based Code Generation using Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: The utilization of programming language (PL) models, pre-trained on large-scale code corpora, as a means of automating software engineering processes has demonstrated considerable potential in streamlining various code generation tasks such as code completion, code translation, and program synthesis. However, current approaches mainly rely on supervised fine-tuning objectives borrowed from text generation, neglecting unique sequence-level characteristics of code, including but not limited to compilability as well as syntactic and functional correctness. To address this limitation, we propose PPOCoder, a new framework for code generation that synergistically combines pre-trained PL models with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) which is a widely used deep reinforcement learning technique. By utilizing non-differentiable feedback from code execution and structure alignment, PPOCoder seamlessly integrates external code-specific knowledge into the model optimization process. It's important to note that PPOCoder is a task-agnostic and model-agnostic framework that can be used across different code generation tasks and PLs. Extensive experiments on three code generation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach compared to SOTA methods, achieving significant improvements in compilation success rates and functional correctness across different PLs.

paper_metadata.title: Will Code Remain a Relevant User Interface for End-User Programming with Generative AI Models?
paper_metadata.abstract: The research field of end-user programming has largely been concerned with helping non-experts learn to code sufficiently well in order to achieve their tasks. Generative AI stands to obviate this entirely by allowing users to generate code from naturalistic language prompts. In this essay, we explore the extent to which "traditional" programming languages remain relevant for non-expert end-user programmers in a world with generative AI. We posit the "generative shift hypothesis": that generative AI will create qualitative and quantitative expansions in the traditional scope of end-user programming. We outline some reasons that traditional programming languages may still be relevant and useful for end-user programmers. We speculate whether each of these reasons might be fundamental and enduring, or whether they may disappear with further improvements and innovations in generative AI. Finally, we articulate a set of implications for end-user programming research, including the possibility of needing to revisit many well-established core concepts, such as Ko's learning barriers and Blackwell's attention investment model.

paper_metadata.title: Synthesis of Reversible Functions Beyond Gate Count and Quantum Cost
paper_metadata.abstract: Many synthesis approaches for reversible and quantum logic have been proposed so far. However, most of them generate circuits with respect to simple metrics, i.e. gate count or quantum cost. On the other hand, to physically realize reversible and quantum hardware, additional constraints exist. In this paper, we describe cost metrics beyond gate count and quantum cost that should be considered while synthesizing reversible and quantum logic for the respective target technologies. We show that the evaluation of a synthesis approach may differ if additional costs are applied. In addition, a new cost metric, namely Nearest Neighbor Cost (NNC) which is imposed by realistic physical quantum architectures, is considered in detail. We discuss how existing synthesis flows can be extended to generate optimal circuits with respect to NNC while still keeping the quantum cost small.

paper_metadata.title: Synth-by-Reg (SbR): Contrastive learning for synthesis-based registration of paired images
paper_metadata.abstract: Nonlinear inter-modality registration is often challenging due to the lack of objective functions that are good proxies for alignment. Here we propose a synthesis-by-registration method to convert this problem into an easier intra-modality task. We introduce a registration loss for weakly supervised image translation between domains that does not require perfectly aligned training data. This loss capitalises on a registration U-Net with frozen weights, to drive a synthesis CNN towards the desired translation. We complement this loss with a structure preserving constraint based on contrastive learning, which prevents blurring and content shifts due to overfitting. We apply this method to the registration of histological sections to MRI slices, a key step in 3D histology reconstruction. Results on two different public datasets show improvements over registration based on mutual information (13% reduction in landmark error) and synthesis-based algorithms such as CycleGAN (11% reduction), and are comparable to a registration CNN with label supervision. Code and data are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/acasamitjana/SynthByReg}

rag_package.related_work_summary: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled their deployment as agents for various user-specified tasks, including code synthesis. A key challenge, however, lies in enabling these LLMs to effectively leverage feedback, particularly execution feedback, to iteratively refine their generations. While general LLM capabilities and evaluations have been explored (Chen et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024), effectively incorporating dynamic feedback for iterative improvement in code generation remains an active area of research. Related work has begun to explore reinforcement learning for execution-based code generation, with approaches like PPOCoder integrating non-differentiable feedback from code execution via Proximal Policy Optimization (Shojaee et al., 2023). The broader implications of generative AI for programming and user interfaces are also being considered (Sarkar, 2023), highlighting the need for robust and adaptive code generation systems. These efforts underscore the difficulty LLMs face in moving beyond independent sampling to achieve reliable outcomes through iterative refinement, particularly on complex tasks like competitive programming.

3.desc: No RAG, 2 iterations, 1 reviewer, AI Detector enabled, no author rebuttal

strengths: The paper introduces an end-to-end reinforcement learning approach (RLEF) for code generation that effectively utilizes execution feedback, a critical component for autonomous agents that has historically been tough to leverage effectively in this domain. This is a very novel and impactful idea.

RLEF achieves substantial performance gains on challenging competitive programming benchmarks (CodeContests, HumanEval+, MBPP+), significantly outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods while using an order of magnitude fewer samples. This demonstrates significant progress in code LLMs.

The in-depth analysis of inference-time behavior, including ablations with random feedback and different turn limits, clearly demonstrates that RLEF-trained models genuinely learn to leverage execution feedback for self-repair, rather than just producing diverse outputs. This insight is crucial for understanding the model's capabilities.
weaknesses: While the concept of grounding LLMs in execution feedback is highly novel, some of the methodological details of the PPO implementation (e.g., the specific reward function design and its interaction with the token-level policy and turn-level value function) could be explained with greater intuition or more detailed analysis of their impact. For instance, the choice of using a token-level policy but a turn-level value function, and the geometric mean for KL calculation, are presented as effective but lack deeper theoretical justification in the main text beyond 'worked best in our early experiments.'

The paper mentions that the RLEF method might reduce the diversity of outputs in some settings, as per related work (Kirk et al., 2024). Further investigation into this trade-off and potential strategies to mitigate it would strengthen the broader applicability of the method, particularly in scenarios where diverse solutions might be desirable.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a bold and genuinely innovative step forward in equipping LLMs with crucial agentic capabilities, specifically the ability to effectively ground their generations in inference-time execution feedback for code synthesis. The RLEF method, an end-to-end reinforcement learning approach, delivers impressive performance gains on highly challenging competitive programming tasks, even outperforming models with significantly larger sample budgets. The strength of this work lies in its novelty and potential to inspire future research in self-correcting and autonomous LLMs. While some minor details in the methodology could benefit from further elaboration, the core idea is sound and the results are highly significant. The analysis provides strong evidence that the models are indeed learning to leverage feedback, which is exactly the kind of forward-thinking contribution we should be celebrating. The potential for this work to generalize to other domains requiring iterative feedback loops is immense. Given that there was no rebuttal, my initial assessment stands. I am very excited about this paper and recommend acceptance.

The use of 'reinforcement learning' (PPO) for optimizing LLMs, particularly when integrated with structured feedback, is a core topic listed in ICML's interests ('reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.)').

The application of machine learning to 'code generation' (a form of 'application-driven machine learning') by effectively leveraging execution feedback, especially showing substantial performance gains on competitive programming, strongly fits the 'innovative techniques' aspect of ICML's application-driven ML category.

why_it_does_not_fit: While the methodological details of PPO are provided, Reviewer 1 notes that 'some of the methodological details... could be explained with greater intuition or more detailed analysis of their impact.' The paper's focus is primarily empirical demonstration of performance gains rather than deep theoretical contributions to the foundations of RL or LLMs, which some ICML papers lean towards.
