paper_metadata.title: A survey: object detection methods from CNN to transformer
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract Object detection is the most important problem in computer vision tasks. After AlexNet proposed, based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) methods have become mainstream in the computer vision field, many researches on neural networks and different transformations of algorithm structures have appeared. In order to achieve fast and accurate detection effects, it is necessary to jump out of the existing CNN framework and has great challenges. Transformer’s relatively mature theoretical support and technological development in the field of Natural Language Processing have brought it into the researcher’s sight, and it has been proved that Transformer’s method can be used for computer vision tasks, and proved that it exceeds the existing CNN method in some tasks. In order to enable more researchers to better understand the development process of object detection methods, existing methods, different frameworks, challenging problems and development trends, paper introduced historical classic methods of object detection used CNN, discusses the highlights, advantages and disadvantages of these algorithms. By consulting a large amount of paper, the paper compared different CNN detection methods and Transformer detection methods. Vertically under fair conditions, 13 different detection methods that have a broad impact on the field and are the most mainstream and promising are selected for comparison. The comparative data gives us confidence in the development of Transformer and the convergence between different methods. It also presents the recent innovative approaches to using Transformer in computer vision tasks. In the end, the challenges, opportunities and future prospects of this field are summarized.

paper_metadata.title: Positional Games and QBF: A Polished Encoding
paper_metadata.abstract: Positional games are a mathematical class of two-player games comprising Tic-tac-toe and its generalizations. We propose a novel encoding of these games into Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBFs) such that a game instance admits a winning strategy for the first player if and only if the corresponding formula is true. Our approach improves over previous QBF encodings of games in multiple ways. First, it is generic and lets us encode other positional games, such as Hex. Second, the structural properties of positional games, together with careful treatment of illegal moves, let us generate more compact instances that can be solved faster by state-of-the-art QBF solvers. We establish the latter fact through extensive experiments. Finally, the compactness of our new encoding makes it feasible to translate realistic game problems. We identify a few such problems of historical significance and put them forward to the QBF community as milestones of increasing difficulty.

paper_metadata.title: Numerical Design of Distributive Mixing Elements
paper_metadata.abstract: This paper presents a novel shape-optimization technique for the design of mixing elements in single-screw extruders. Extruders enable the continuous production of constant-cross-section profiles. Equipped with one or several screw-shaped rotors, extruders transport polymer particles towards the outlet. Due to shear heating, melting is induced and a melt stream is created, which can be further processed. While many variants of multi-screw extruders exist, a significant share of all extrusion machines is made up of single-screw extruders due to their comparatively low operating costs and complexity. While the reduced complexity yields economic benefits, single-screw extruders' mixing capabilities, i.e., their ability to produce a melt with a homogeneous material and temperature distribution, suffer compared to multi-screw extruders. To compensate for this shortcoming, so-called mixing elements are added to the screw to enhance mixing by recurring flow reorientations. In view of the largely unintuitive flow characteristics of polymer melts, we present an optimization framework that allows designing these mixing elements numerically based on finite-element simulations of the melt flow. To reduce the computational demand required by shape optimization of a complete mixing section, we only focus on the shape optimization of a single mixing element. This paper presents advances in three aspects of numerical design: (1) A combination of free-form deformation and surface splines is presented, allowing to parameterize the mixing element's shape by very few variables. (2) The combination of this concept with a linear-elasticity-based mesh update method to deform the computational domain without the need for remeshing is demonstrated. (3) A simple yet robust and sensitive objective formulation to assess distributive mixing in laminar flows based on a measure for the interfacial area is proposed.

paper_metadata.title: Exploring Feasible Design Spaces for Heterogeneous Constraints
paper_metadata.abstract: We demonstrate an approach of exploring design spaces to simultaneously satisfy kinematics- and physics-based requirements. We present a classification of constraints and solvers to enable postponing optimization as far down the design workflow as possible. The solvers are organized into two broad classes of design space 'pruning' and 'exploration' by considering the types of constraints they can satisfy. We show that pointwise constraints define feasible design subspaces that can be represented and computed as first-class entities by their maximal feasible elements. The design space is pruned upfront by intersecting maximal elements, without premature optimization. To solve for other constraints, we apply topology optimization (TO), starting from the pruned feasible space. The optimization is steered by a topological sensitivity field (TSF) that measures the global changes in violation of constraints with respect to local topological punctures. The TSF for global objective functions is augmented with TSF for global constraints, and penalized/filtered to incorporate local constraints, including set constraints converted to differentiable (in)equality constraints. We demonstrate application of the proposed workflow to nontrivial examples in design and manufacturing. Among other examples, we show how to explore pruned design spaces via TO to simultaneously satisfy physics-based constraints (e.g., minimize compliance and mass) as well as kinematics-based constraints (e.g., maximize accessibility for machining).

paper_metadata.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
paper_metadata.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models, and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths. Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information. We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position. Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism, but also from the effects of the causal mask.

paper_metadata.title: Evaluation of Software Product Quality Metrics
paper_metadata.abstract: Computing devices and associated software govern everyday life, and form the backbone of safety critical systems in banking, healthcare, automotive and other fields. Increasing system complexity, quickly evolving technologies and paradigm shifts have kept software quality research at the forefront. Standards such as ISO's 25010 express it in terms of sub-characteristics such as maintainability, reliability and security. A significant body of literature attempts to link these subcharacteristics with software metric values, with the end goal of creating a metric-based model of software product quality. However, research also identifies the most important existing barriers. Among them we mention the diversity of software application types, development platforms and languages. Additionally, unified definitions to make software metrics truly language-agnostic do not exist, and would be difficult to implement given programming language levels of variety. This is compounded by the fact that many existing studies do not detail their methodology and tooling, which precludes researchers from creating surveys to enable data analysis on a larger scale. In our paper, we propose a comprehensive study of metric values in the context of three complex, open-source applications. We align our methodology and tooling with that of existing research, and present it in detail in order to facilitate comparative evaluation. We study metric values during the entire 18-year development history of our target applications, in order to capture the longitudinal view that we found lacking in existing literature. We identify metric dependencies and check their consistency across applications and their versions. At each step, we carry out comparative evaluation with existing research and present our results.

paper_metadata.title: Mixed-precision finite element kernels and assembly: Rounding error analysis and hardware acceleration
paper_metadata.abstract: In this paper we develop the first fine-grained rounding error analysis of finite element (FE) cell kernels and assembly. The theory includes mixed-precision implementations and accounts for hardware-acceleration via matrix multiplication units, thus providing theoretical guidance for designing reduced- and mixed-precision FE algorithms on CPUs and GPUs. Guided by this analysis, we introduce hardware-accelerated mixed-precision implementation strategies which are provably robust to low-precision computations. Indeed, these algorithms are accurate to the lower-precision unit roundoff with an error constant that is independent from: the conditioning of FE basis function evaluations, the ill-posedness of the cell, the polynomial degree, and the number of quadrature nodes. Consequently, we present the first AMX-accelerated FE kernel implementations on Intel Sapphire Rapids CPUs. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed mixed- (single/half-) precision algorithms are up to 60 times faster than their double precision equivalent while being orders of magnitude more accurate than their fully half-precision counterparts.

paper_metadata.title: Expressivity and Speech Synthesis
paper_metadata.abstract: Imbuing machines with the ability to talk has been a longtime pursuit of artificial intelligence (AI) research. From the very beginning, the community has not only aimed to synthesise high-fidelity speech that accurately conveys the semantic meaning of an utterance, but also to colour it with inflections that cover the same range of affective expressions that humans are capable of. After many years of research, it appears that we are on the cusp of achieving this when it comes to single, isolated utterances. This unveils an abundance of potential avenues to explore when it comes to combining these single utterances with the aim of synthesising more complex, longer-term behaviours. In the present chapter, we outline the methodological advances that brought us so far and sketch out the ongoing efforts to reach that coveted next level of artificial expressivity. We also discuss the societal implications coupled with rapidly advancing expressive speech synthesis (ESS) technology and highlight ways to mitigate those risks and ensure the alignment of ESS capabilities with ethical norms.

strengths: The paper tackles a highly significant and under-explored area: the expressivity limits of Transformers under realistic, fixed-precision arithmetic. This moves beyond idealized theoretical models and brings the discussion closer to practical implementations.

The core finding that fixed-precision Transformers (without PE and with Assumption 5.1) are limited to finite or co-finite languages is a bold and potentially paradigm-shifting result. It suggests that many real-world Transformers might behave as little more than efficient lookup tables, which has profound implications for understanding their capabilities.

The paper systematically investigates the impact of various constraints (fixed-precision, positional encoding, and assumption on query-key parameters) on expressivity, offering insights into where the limitations stem from. The table summarizing upper and lower bounds is very helpful.

The explicit definition of what constitutes a language recognized by a Transformer decoder, including autoregressive generation and acceptance conditions, is well-articulated and provides a solid basis for theoretical analysis.
weaknesses: While the theoretical proofs (especially for the upper bound) are presented, the level of detail is somewhat condensed, particularly in the lower bound proofs where the construction of transformer components (e.g., FFNs for specific tasks) is described at a high level. More rigorous, step-by-step constructions would strengthen the soundness of these claims.

The evaluation aspect is purely theoretical. While this is common in expressivity papers, the bold claims about 'practical Transformers' functioning as 'efficient lookup tables' would benefit from a discussion of how these theoretical limitations might manifest in empirical benchmarks or actual model behavior, even if not a full experimental section.

The 'proof sketches' for the lower bounds (especially 6.1 and 6.2) are rather high-level. While the idea is clear, a more thorough mathematical demonstration of how these specific language classes are constructed with fixed-precision arithmetic, without running into the previous limitations, would be valuable. strengths: The paper tackles a fundamentally important question regarding the real-world expressivity of Transformers under practical constraints, moving beyond idealized theoretical models. strengths: The paper provides rigorous mathematical proofs for the theoretical expressivity bounds of fixed-precision Transformers under various conditions, which is crucial for understanding their fundamental limitations.

weaknesses: While the theoretical rigor is commendable, the proofs, particularly for the lower bounds, involve specific constructions of Transformer components that might be difficult to translate into practical model design choices for achieving the stated expressivity. However, a slightly more detailed explanation or motivation for certain design choices in these definitions (e.g., the specific inclusion of +inf, -inf, nan, and the 'p-space-bounded Turing machine' for functions) could further enhance clarity for readers less familiar with this specific formalization.

The systematic analysis of surrogate gradient slopes, particularly the proposed adaptive scheduling, is an innovative way to balance exploration and exploitation in SNNs, showing a clear performance boost. The novel TD3BC+JSRL framework, combining privileged guiding policies with online SNN interaction, is a bold solution to the 'warm-up period' problem in real-world robotics. The successful application to drone flight, with significant outperformance of conventional methods and successful sim-to-real transfer, speaks volumes about its practical significance. Minor methodological imperfections in the theoretical derivations and the stark performance gap with baselines do not detract from the core novelty and the potential to unlock new frontiers for energy-efficient neuromorphic controllers. target_paper_summary.title: Adaptive Surrogate Gradients For Sequential Reinforcement Learning In Spiking Neural Networks
target_paper_summary.abstract:
Neuromorphic computing systems are set to revolutionize energy-constrained robotics by achieving orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains, while enabling native temporal processing. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) represent a promising algorithmic approach for these systems, yet their application to complex control tasks faces two critical challenges: (1) the non-differentiable nature of spiking neurons necessitates surrogate gradients with unclear optimization properties, and (2) the stateful dynamics of SNNs require training on sequences, which in reinforcement learning (RL) is hindered by limited sequence lengths during early training, preventing the network from bridging its warm-up period.

We address these challenges by systematically analyzing surrogate gradient slope settings, showing that shallower slopes increase gradient magnitude in deeper layers but reduce alignment with true gradients. In supervised learning, we find no clear preference for fixed or scheduled slopes. The effect is much more pronounced in RL settings, where shallower slopes or scheduled slopes lead to a ×2.1 improvement in both training and final deployed performance. Next, we propose a novel training approach that leverages a privileged guiding policy to bootstrap the learning process, while still exploiting online environment interactions with the spiking policy. Combining our method with an adaptive slope schedule for a real-world drone position control task, we achieve an average return of 400 points, substantially outperforming prior techniques, including Behavioral Cloning and TD3BC, which achieve at most –200 points under the same conditions. This work advances both the theoretical understanding of surrogate gradient learning in SNNs and practical training methodologies for neuromorphic controllers demonstrated in real-world robotic systems.

paper_metadata.title: Synaptic metaplasticity in binarized neural networks
paper_metadata.abstract: While deep neural networks have surpassed human performance in multiple situations, they are prone to catastrophic forgetting: upon training a new task, they rapidly forget previously learned ones. Neuroscience studies, based on idealized tasks, suggest that in the brain, synapses overcome this issue by adjusting their plasticity depending on their past history. However, such "metaplastic" behaviors do not transfer directly to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in deep neural networks. In this work, we interpret the hidden weights used by binarized neural networks, a low-precision version of deep neural networks, as metaplastic variables, and modify their training technique to alleviate forgetting. Building on this idea, we propose and demonstrate experimentally, in situations of multitask and stream learning, a training technique that reduces catastrophic forgetting without needing previously presented data, nor formal boundaries between datasets and with performance approaching more mainstream techniques with task boundaries. We support our approach with a theoretical analysis on a tractable task. This work bridges computational neuroscience and deep learning, and presents significant assets for future embedded and neuromorphic systems, especially when using novel nanodevices featuring physics analogous to metaplasticity.

paper_metadata.title: Memristors -- from In-memory computing, Deep Learning Acceleration, Spiking Neural Networks, to the Future of Neuromorphic and Bio-inspired Computing
paper_metadata.abstract: Machine learning, particularly in the form of deep learning, has driven most of the recent fundamental developments in artificial intelligence. Deep learning is based on computational models that are, to a certain extent, bio-inspired, as they rely on networks of connected simple computing units operating in parallel. Deep learning has been successfully applied in areas such as object/pattern recognition, speech and natural language processing, self-driving vehicles, intelligent self-diagnostics tools, autonomous robots, knowledgeable personal assistants, and monitoring. These successes have been mostly supported by three factors: availability of vast amounts of data, continuous growth in computing power, and algorithmic innovations. The approaching demise of Moore's law, and the consequent expected modest improvements in computing power that can be achieved by scaling, raise the question of whether the described progress will be slowed or halted due to hardware limitations. This paper reviews the case for a novel beyond CMOS hardware technology, memristors, as a potential solution for the implementation of power-efficient in-memory computing, deep learning accelerators, and spiking neural networks. Central themes are the reliance on non-von-Neumann computing architectures and the need for developing tailored learning and inference algorithms. To argue that lessons from biology can be useful in providing directions for further progress in artificial intelligence, we briefly discuss an example based reservoir computing. We conclude the review by speculating on the big picture view of future neuromorphic and brain-inspired computing systems.

rag_package.related_work_summary: Recent advancements in neuromorphic computing emphasize the potential of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) for energy-efficient AI, especially in robotics. The development of specialized hardware like memristors is crucial for achieving high efficiency in these systems, enabling in-memory computing, Deep Learning acceleration, and SNN implementations (Mehonic et al., 2020). However, training SNNs for complex tasks presents unique challenges, including the non-differentiable nature of spiking neurons and the need for robust handling of sequential data. Efforts are also being made to address fundamental problems in neural network training, such as catastrophic forgetting, through innovations like metaplasticity in binarized neural networks, which can apply to the broader field of neuromorphic systems (Laborieux et al., 2021). Our work builds upon these foundations by systematically analyzing adaptive surrogate gradients for sequential reinforcement learning in SNNs, aiming to enhance the stability and performance of neuromorphic controllers in real-world applications.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel approach by combining adaptive surrogate gradients with a privileged guiding policy (TD3BC+JSRL) to overcome critical SNN training challenges in RL, especially the 'warm-up period' issue in real-world robotics. This is a genuinely creative solution to a hard problem.

The systematic analysis of surrogate gradient slopes, particularly the insight that shallower slopes increase gradient magnitude in deeper layers at the cost of alignment but are beneficial for RL exploration, is a significant theoretical contribution. The adaptive scheduling strategy for these slopes is also a clever innovation that balances exploration and exploitation.

The practical demonstration on a real-world drone control task, successfully bridging the sim-to-real gap without explicit action history (unlike ANNs), showcases the strong potential and real-world applicability of the method. The dramatic performance improvement over baselines (from -200 to 400 points) is highly compelling.
weaknesses: While the paper clearly states the benefits of the adaptive slope schedule, the exact mechanisms and hyperparameters for the 'adaptive' schedule (Equation 7) could be elaborated more, particularly how 'r' and 'r′' are specifically computed in practice for a continuous control task beyond just discrete rewards, ensuring its robustness across varying reward landscapes.

The 'asymmetric actor-critic' setup uses an ANN critic and a spiking actor. While this is a practical choice for stability, it limits the full 'neuromorphic' purity of the system. Future work should ideally aim for a fully spiking critic, or at least a more thorough discussion of the implications of this hybrid architecture for energy efficiency, given the SNN's core advantage.
reviewers.summary_comment:

I am particularly impressed by the systematic analysis of surrogate gradients, revealing practical insights into how steepness affects deep network training in both supervised learning and RL. The proposed adaptive scheduling for these gradients is a clever mechanism to balance exploration and exploitation, which is a common challenge in RL. The results on the Crazyflie drone, demonstrating superior performance and sim-to-real transfer over strong baselines, provide compelling evidence for the efficacy and practical significance of this work. The ability of the SNN to control the drone without explicit action history, unlike its ANN counterpart, further highlights its potential for energy-efficient, natively temporal processing.

While there are minor areas for further detail (e.g., precise adaptive slope implementation details, full neuromorphic architecture for the critic), these do not detract from the bold, forward-thinking nature and significant potential impact of the presented research. The authors have effectively pushed the boundaries of SNN applications in demanding robotic environments. This paper should inspire much future work in this critical area. My review remains unchanged as no rebuttal was provided to address the identified points.

The evaluation is thorough, including comparisons with relevant baselines (BC, TD3BC, TD3), an ablation study, and real-world deployment on a Crazyflie quadrotor, demonstrating strong empirical evidence for the proposed methods' efficacy and practical transferability.
weaknesses: While the paper analyzes the impact of surrogate gradients, a deeper theoretical analysis of the adaptive scheduling strategy, particularly regarding its optimality or convergence properties, could further strengthen the soundness.

The reliance on a 'privileged guiding policy' as a prerequisite, while practical for enabling training, is a limitation. The paper acknowledges this but could explore systematic ways to obtain or robustify this guide when an expert is not readily available.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a strong contribution to the field of Spiking Neural Networks, particularly its application to Reinforcement Learning for continuous control. The systematic analysis of surrogate gradients, dissecting the trade-offs between slope, gradient magnitude, and alignment, is commendable and provides much-needed theoretical insight. The proposed TD3BC+JSRL method is a well-conceived solution to the challenging problem of training SNNs on sequential tasks in environments with high early failure rates. The extensive evaluation, including real-world experiments on a Crazyflie drone and a detailed ablation study, provides convincing evidence of the method's effectiveness and practical relevance. The results clearly demonstrate a substantial improvement over existing methods. The paper is well-written, and the authors make efforts to ensure reproducibility with provided code. The primary areas for improvement would be a more in-depth theoretical justification for the adaptive slope scheduling and a discussion on strategies for obtaining the guiding policy in more general scenarios. Overall, this is a methodologically sound and empirically validated work that advances the state of the art in neuromorphic control.

strengths: The paper tackles a highly practical and relevant problem: enabling SNNs for real-world, energy-constrained robotics, particularly in challenging control tasks like drone flight. Its focus on enabling native temporal processing for SNNs without inefficient workarounds like frame-stacking is a significant practical advantage.

The combination of a thorough analysis of surrogate gradient slopes with a novel RL training methodology (TD3BC+JSRL) is a powerful approach. The empirical demonstration of a 600-point reward gap over baselines on a real-world drone task, including successful sim-to-real transfer, strongly validates the proposed method's effectiveness.

The paper provides excellent insight into the challenges of SNN training, including the non-differentiable nature of spiking neurons and the warm-up period for stateful dynamics. The adaptive slope scheduling and the jump-start framework directly address these practical hurdles, making SNNs more amenable to deep RL in complex environments. The NeuroBench comparison and energy efficiency discussion further highlight the practical benefits.
weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges the need for a 'stable guiding policy' in the TD3BC+JSRL framework, it doesn't delve much into the effort or complexity required to obtain such a policy, particularly in novel, high-risk environments where the SNN might be most needed. This could be a significant practical hurdle for practitioners.

The discussion on the 'asymmetric actor-critic' where the critic is an ANN and receives 'privileged information' (action histories) while the SNN does not, could be further elaborated. While it aids training stability, the practical implications for deploying a hybrid system or the disparity in input information between actor and critic in a real-world scenario could be clearer, especially regarding whether the 'privileged information' is truly available during real-time drone operation for the critic if it were deployed.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper addresses critical challenges in training Spiking Neural Networks for practical, real-world robotic control, specifically focusing on energy-efficient drone flight. The dual contribution of analyzing surrogate gradient behavior and proposing a novel RL training framework (TD3BC+JSRL) is highly significant. The empirical results on a Crazyflie drone, demonstrating superior performance and successful sim-to-real transfer compared to strong baselines, provide compelling evidence of the method's practical utility. The work clearly communicates its motivation, methodology, and results, making it highly valuable for practitioners and researchers in neuromorphic computing and robotics. The discussion of energy efficiency and comparison with ANNs further solidifies its practical impact. While some aspects of the guiding policy and asymmetric actor-critic could benefit from further elaboration on practical implementation challenges, the paper's overall strengths in significance, evaluation, and clarity make it a strong contribution.

target_paper_summary.title: Learning Linear Attention In Polynomial Time
target_paper_summary.abstract: Previous research has explored the expressivity of Transformer models in simulating Boolean circuits or Turing machines. However, the efficient learnability of Transformers from data has remained an open question. Our study addresses this gap by providing the first polynomial-time learnability results (specifically strong, agnostic PAC learning) for single-layer Transformers with linear attention. We show that learning the optimal multi head linear attention can be recast as finding the optimal kernel predictor in a suitably defined RKHS. Moving to generalization, we construct an algorithm that, given a dataset, checks in polynomial time whether the set of best fit multi head linear attention networks on this data all perform an identical computation–a powerful notion for out of distribution generalization. We empirically validate our theoretical findings on several canonical tasks: learning random linear attention networks, key–value associations, and learning to execute finite automata. Our findings bridge a critical gap between theoretical expressivity and learnability of Transformer models.

paper_metadata.title: Space-time distributions
paper_metadata.abstract: The space-time foliation Sigma compatible with the gravitational field g on a 4-manifold M determines a fibration pi of M, pi : M -> N is a surjective submersion over the 1-dimensional leaves space N. M is then written as a disjoint union of the leaves of Sigma, which are 3-dimensional spacelike surfaces on M. The decomposition, TM=Sigma + T^0 M, also implies that we can define a lift of the curves on N to curves (non-spacelike) on M. The stable causality condition M coincides with Sigma being a causal space-time distribution, generated by an exact timelike 1-form omega^0 = dt where t is some real function on M. In this case M is written as a disjoint union of a family of spacelike 3-surfaces of constant t, which cover D^+(S) of a initial 3-surface S of M.

paper_metadata.title: A Polynomial time Algorithm for 3SAT
paper_metadata.abstract: By creating some new concepts and methods: checking tree, long unit path, direct contradiction unit pair, indirect contradiction unit pair, additional contradiction unit pair, 2-unit layer and 3-unit layer, redundant units, and destroying parallel pairs , we successfully transform solving a 3SAT problem to solving 2SAT problems in polynomial time. Thus we proved that NP=P.

paper_metadata.title: Self-Attention through Kernel-Eigen Pair Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes
paper_metadata.abstract: While the great capability of Transformers significantly boosts prediction accuracy, it could also yield overconfident predictions and require calibrated uncertainty estimation, which can be commonly tackled by Gaussian processes (GPs). Existing works apply GPs with symmetric kernels under variational inference to the attention kernel; however, omitting the fact that attention kernels are in essence asymmetric. Moreover, the complexity of deriving the GP posteriors remains high for large-scale data. In this work, we propose Kernel-Eigen Pair Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes (KEP-SVGP) for building uncertainty-aware self-attention where the asymmetry of attention kernels is tackled by Kernel SVD (KSVD) and a reduced complexity is acquired. Through KEP-SVGP, i) the SVGP pair induced by the two sets of singular vectors from KSVD w.r.t. the attention kernel fully characterizes the asymmetry; ii) using only a small set of adjoint eigenfunctions from KSVD, the derivation of SVGP posteriors can be based on the inversion of a diagonal matrix containing singular values, contributing to a reduction in time complexity; iii) an evidence lower bound is derived so that variational parameters and network weights can be optimized with it. Experiments verify our excellent performances and efficiency on in-distribution, distribution-shift and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

paper_metadata.title: Primal-Attention: Self-attention through Asymmetric Kernel SVD in Primal Representation
paper_metadata.abstract: Recently, a new line of works has emerged to understand and improve self-attention in Transformers by treating it as a kernel machine. However, existing works apply the methods for symmetric kernels to the asymmetric self-attention, resulting in a nontrivial gap between the analytical understanding and numerical implementation. In this paper, we provide a new perspective to represent and optimize self-attention through asymmetric Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD), which is also motivated by the low-rank property of self-attention normally observed in deep layers. Through asymmetric KSVD, $i$) a primal-dual representation of self-attention is formulated, where the optimization objective is cast to maximize the projection variances in the attention outputs; $ii$) a novel attention mechanism, i.e., Primal-Attention, is proposed via the primal representation of KSVD, avoiding explicit computation of the kernel matrix in the dual; $iii$) with KKT conditions, we prove that the stationary solution to the KSVD optimization in Primal-Attention yields a zero-value objective. In this manner, KSVD optimization can be implemented by simply minimizing a regularization loss, so that low-rank property is promoted without extra decomposition. Numerical experiments show state-of-the-art performance of our Primal-Attention with improved efficiency. Moreover, we demonstrate that the deployed KSVD optimization regularizes Primal-Attention with a sharper singular value decay than that of the canonical self-attention, further verifying the great potential of our method. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that provides a primal-dual representation for the asymmetric kernel in self-attention and successfully applies it to modeling and optimization.

paper_metadata.title: On the Sample Complexity of Adversarial Multi-Source PAC Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: We study the problem of learning from multiple untrusted data sources, a scenario of increasing practical relevance given the recent emergence of crowdsourcing and collaborative learning paradigms. Specifically, we analyze the situation in which a learning system obtains datasets from multiple sources, some of which might be biased or even adversarially perturbed. It is known that in the single-source case, an adversary with the power to corrupt a fixed fraction of the training data can prevent PAC-learnability, that is, even in the limit of infinitely much training data, no learning system can approach the optimal test error. In this work we show that, surprisingly, the same is not true in the multi-source setting, where the adversary can arbitrarily corrupt a fixed fraction of the data sources. Our main results are a generalization bound that provides finite-sample guarantees for this learning setting, as well as corresponding lower bounds. Besides establishing PAC-learnability our results also show that in a cooperative learning setting sharing data with other parties has provable benefits, even if some participants are malicious.

paper_metadata.title: Beyond Self-attention: External Attention using Two Linear Layers for Visual Tasks
paper_metadata.abstract: Attention mechanisms, especially self-attention, have played an increasingly important role in deep feature representation for visual tasks. Self-attention updates the feature at each position by computing a weighted sum of features using pair-wise affinities across all positions to capture the long-range dependency within a single sample. However, self-attention has quadratic complexity and ignores potential correlation between different samples. This paper proposes a novel attention mechanism which we call external attention, based on two external, small, learnable, shared memories, which can be implemented easily by simply using two cascaded linear layers and two normalization layers; it conveniently replaces self-attention in existing popular architectures. External attention has linear complexity and implicitly considers the correlations between all data samples. We further incorporate the multi-head mechanism into external attention to provide an all-MLP architecture, external attention MLP (EAMLP), for image classification. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, image generation, and point cloud analysis reveal that our method provides results comparable or superior to the self-attention mechanism and some of its variants, with much lower computational and memory costs.

paper_metadata.title: Superiority of Multi-Head Attention in In-Context Linear Regression
paper_metadata.abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of the performance of transformer with softmax attention in in-context learning with linear regression tasks. While the existing literature predominantly focuses on the convergence of transformers with single-/multi-head attention, our research centers on comparing their performance. We conduct an exact theoretical analysis to demonstrate that multi-head attention with a substantial embedding dimension performs better than single-head attention. When the number of in-context examples D increases, the prediction loss using single-/multi-head attention is in O(1/D), and the one for multi-head attention has a smaller multiplicative constant. In addition to the simplest data distribution setting, we consider more scenarios, e.g., noisy labels, local examples, correlated features, and prior knowledge. We observe that, in general, multi-head attention is preferred over single-head attention. Our results verify the effectiveness of the design of multi-head attention in the transformer architecture.

rag_package.related_work_summary: While previous research has explored the expressivity of Transformer models, the efficient learnability from data, particularly in polynomial time, has remained an underserved area. Our work provides the first polynomial-time learnability results for single-layer Transformers with linear attention, contrasting with generalized notions of polynomial time algorithms such as those applied to 3SAT problems (Du, 2010). Our approach recasts learning optimal multi-head linear attention as finding an optimal kernel predictor in a suitably defined RKHS. This methodology is related to recent advancements employing kernel methods for understanding and improving self-attention, such as using Kernel-Eigen Pair Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes for uncertainty-aware self-attention (Chen et al., 2024) and leveraging asymmetric Kernel SVD in a primal representation for self-attention (Chen et al., 2023). Our PAC learning framework is distinct from prior PAC learning work that has focused on challenges in adversarial multi-source settings (Konstantinov et al., 2020), which has explored the sample complexity in such scenarios. Furthermore, our focus on multi-head linear attention builds upon understandings of multi-head attention, for example, its theoretical superiority in in-context linear regression tasks (Cui et al., 2024), while other related works explore alternative attention mechanisms like external attention with linear complexity for visual tasks (Guo et al., 2021).

target_paper_summary.title: Class-Wise Balancing Data Replay For Federated Class-Incremental Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract:
Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL) aims to collaboratively process continuously increasing incoming tasks across multiple clients. Among various approaches, data replay has become a promising solution, which can alleviate forgetting by reintroducing representative samples from previous tasks. However, their performance is typically limited by class imbalance, both within the replay buffer due to limited global awareness and between replayed and newly arrived classes. To address this issue, we propose a class-wise balancing data replay method for FCIL (FedCBDR), which employs a global coordination mechanism for class-level memory construction and reweights the learning objective to alleviate the aforementioned imbalances. Specifically, FedCBDR has two key components:
1) the global-perspective data replay module reconstructs global representations of prior task in a privacy-preserving manner, which then guides a class-aware and importance-sensitive sampling strategy to achieve balanced replay; 2) Subsequently, to handle class imbalance across tasks, the task-aware temperature scaling module adaptively adjusts the temperature of logits at both class and instance levels based on task dynamics, which reduces the model's overconfidence in majority classes while enhancing its sensitivity to minority classes. Experimental results verified that FedCBDR achieves balanced class-wise sampling under heterogeneous data distributions and improves generalization under task imbalance between earlier and recent tasks, yielding a 2%-15% Top-1 accuracy improvement over six stateof-the-art methods.

paper_metadata.title: Queue-based Resampling for Online Class Imbalance Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Online class imbalance learning constitutes a new problem and an emerging research topic that focusses on the challenges of online learning under class imbalance and concept drift. Class imbalance deals with data streams that have very skewed distributions while concept drift deals with changes in the class imbalance status. Little work exists that addresses these challenges and in this paper we introduce queue-based resampling, a novel algorithm that successfully addresses the co-existence of class imbalance and concept drift. The central idea of the proposed resampling algorithm is to selectively include in the training set a subset of the examples that appeared in the past. Results on two popular benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of queue-based resampling over state-of-the-art methods in terms of learning speed and quality.

paper_metadata.title: A New Strategy of Cost-Free Learning in the Class Imbalance Problem
paper_metadata.abstract: In this work, we define cost-free learning (CFL) formally in comparison with cost-sensitive learning (CSL). The main difference between them is that a CFL approach seeks optimal classification results without requiring any cost information, even in the class imbalance problem. In fact, several CFL approaches exist in the related studies, such as sampling and some criteria-based pproaches. However, to our best knowledge, none of the existing CFL and CSL approaches are able to process the abstaining classifications properly when no information is given about errors and rejects. Based on information theory, we propose a novel CFL which seeks to maximize normalized mutual information of the targets and the decision outputs of classifiers. Using the strategy, we can deal with binary/multi-class classifications with/without abstaining. Significant features are observed from the new strategy. While the degree of class imbalance is changing, the proposed strategy is able to balance the errors and rejects accordingly and automatically. Another advantage of the strategy is its ability of deriving optimal rejection thresholds for abstaining classifications and the "equivalent" costs in binary classifications. The connection between rejection thresholds and ROC curve is explored. Empirical investigation is made on several benchmark data sets in comparison with other existing approaches. The classification results demonstrate a promising perspective of the strategy in machine learning.

paper_metadata.title: Federated and Transfer Learning: A Survey on Adversaries and Defense Mechanisms
paper_metadata.abstract: The advent of federated learning has facilitated large-scale data exchange amongst machine learning models while maintaining privacy. Despite its brief history, federated learning is rapidly evolving to make wider use more practical. One of the most significant advancements in this domain is the incorporation of transfer learning into federated learning, which overcomes fundamental constraints of primary federated learning, particularly in terms of security. This chapter performs a comprehensive survey on the intersection of federated and transfer learning from a security point of view. The main goal of this study is to uncover potential vulnerabilities and defense mechanisms that might compromise the privacy and performance of systems that use federated and transfer learning.

paper_metadata.title: VAFL: a Method of Vertical Asynchronous Federated Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Horizontal Federated learning (FL) handles multi-client data that share the same set of features, and vertical FL trains a better predictor that combine all the features from different clients. This paper targets solving vertical FL in an asynchronous fashion, and develops a simple FL method. The new method allows each client to run stochastic gradient algorithms without coordination with other clients, so it is suitable for intermittent connectivity of clients. This method further uses a new technique of perturbed local embedding to ensure data privacy and improve communication efficiency. Theoretically, we present the convergence rate and privacy level of our method for strongly convex, nonconvex and even nonsmooth objectives separately. Empirically, we apply our method to FL on various image and healthcare datasets. The results compare favorably to centralized and synchronous FL methods.

paper_metadata.title: FastSecAgg: Scalable Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Recent attacks on federated learning demonstrate that keeping the training data on clients' devices does not provide sufficient privacy, as the model parameters shared by clients can leak information about their training data. A 'secure aggregation' protocol enables the server to aggregate clients' models in a privacy-preserving manner. However, existing secure aggregation protocols incur high computation/communication costs, especially when the number of model parameters is larger than the number of clients participating in an iteration -- a typical scenario in federated learning. In this paper, we propose a secure aggregation protocol, FastSecAgg, that is efficient in terms of computation and communication, and robust to client dropouts. The main building block of FastSecAgg is a novel multi-secret sharing scheme, FastShare, based on the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), which may be of independent interest. FastShare is information-theoretically secure, and achieves a trade-off between the number of secrets, privacy threshold, and dropout tolerance. Riding on the capabilities of FastShare, we prove that FastSecAgg is (i) secure against the server colluding with 'any' subset of some constant fraction (e.g. $\sim10\%$) of the clients in the honest-but-curious setting; and (ii) tolerates dropouts of a 'random' subset of some constant fraction (e.g. $\sim10\%$) of the clients. FastSecAgg achieves significantly smaller computation cost than existing schemes while achieving the same (orderwise) communication cost. In addition, it guarantees security against adaptive adversaries, which can perform client corruptions dynamically during the execution of the protocol.

paper_metadata.title: Adaptive Aggregation Networks for Class-Incremental Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn a classification model with the number of classes increasing phase-by-phase. An inherent problem in CIL is the stability-plasticity dilemma between the learning of old and new classes, i.e., high-plasticity models easily forget old classes, but high-stability models are weak to learn new classes. We alleviate this issue by proposing a novel network architecture called Adaptive Aggregation Networks (AANets), in which we explicitly build two types of residual blocks at each residual level (taking ResNet as the baseline architecture): a stable block and a plastic block. We aggregate the output feature maps from these two blocks and then feed the results to the next-level blocks. We adapt the aggregation weights in order to balance these two types of blocks, i.e., to balance stability and plasticity, dynamically. We conduct extensive experiments on three CIL benchmarks: CIFAR-100, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet, and show that many existing CIL methods can be straightforwardly incorporated into the architecture of AANets to boost their performances.

rag_package.related_work_summary: Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL) faces significant challenges, particularly class imbalance within data replay mechanisms, which often limits the performance of existing data replay-based solutions. While online class imbalance learning has been explored, Malialis et al. (2018) propose queue-based resampling to address skewed distributions and concept drift through selective inclusion of past examples. Similarly, Zhang and Hu (2013) offer a cost-free learning strategy for class imbalance, demonstrating the broader interest in balancing techniques. In the context of incremental learning more generally, the stability-plasticity dilemma remains a core issue, as discussed by Liu et al. (2020), who introduce Adaptive Aggregation Networks to balance learning old and new classes. A critical constraint in federated settings, highlighted in this work, is the need for privacy-preserving mechanisms; Kadhe et al. (2020) contribute to this area with FastSecAgg for scalable secure aggregation in federated learning. Broader surveys on federated learning, such as Hallaji et al. (2022), offer insights into general adversarial and defense mechanisms. While our work specifically addresses class-wise balancing data replay in FCIL through global coordination and reweighting, existing methods provide valuable context regarding class imbalance, incremental learning challenges, and privacy considerations in distributed settings.

strengths: The core idea of combining a global-perspective data replay (GDR) with task-aware temperature scaling (TTS) to address class imbalance in Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL) is highly novel and innovative. The use of SVD for privacy-preserving global feature aggregation is particularly creative.

The paper introduces a two-pronged approach, tackling both class-level imbalance within the replay buffer (GDR) and imbalance between replayed and new classes during training (TTS). This comprehensive strategy is significant for advancing FCIL research.

The experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements (2%-15% Top-1 accuracy) over state-of-the-art methods across various datasets and heterogeneity levels, indicating the practical effectiveness and robustness of FedCBDR.
weaknesses: While the concept of using SVD for privacy-preserving global feature aggregation is innovative, the practical computational overhead of performing SVD on large numbers of pseudo-features for every communication round could still be a consideration in extremely large-scale FL scenarios, especially if 'N' (total pseudo-features) grows significantly beyond what was tested.

The sensitivity analysis for the hyperparameters of the TTS module indicates that performance can vary considerably with different settings. This suggests that tuning these parameters might be challenging in real-world deployments and could limit generalizability without robust auto-tuning mechanisms.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly novel and ambitious approach to Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL). The combination of a 'global-perspective data replay' module using SVD for privacy-preserving feature aggregation and a 'task-aware temperature scaling' module for dynamic confidence calibration is highly creative and addresses critical challenges in FCIL, namely class imbalance and catastrophic forgetting. The concept of gaining a global understanding of data distribution without violating privacy through feature space decomposition is a standout feature. The authors' responses have clarified the empirical computational costs and acknowledged the limitations of SVD scalability for extremely large N, and the hyperparameter sensitivity, while also proposing relevant future work directions. This demonstrates a thoughtful and forward-looking approach to addressing the concerns. The substantial performance gains over existing methods underscore its significance. I believe this work will inspire a new wave of research at the intersection of FL and continual learning. The authors explicitly discuss limitations, which is appreciated.

why_it_fits: The paper's topic, Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL) and catastrophic forgetting, falls directly under 'general machine learning' and 'trustworthy machine learning' (reliability) topics, which are central to ICML.

Reviewer A highlights the 'highly novel and innovative' core idea and the 'particularly creative' use of SVD for privacy-preserving global feature aggregation, indicating a strong novelty fit for ICML, which prioritizes cutting-edge research.

The paper explicitly discusses limitations and future work, including computational overhead and hyperparameter sensitivity, which fosters transparency and aligns with ICML's emphasis on thorough scientific discourse.

The problem of class imbalance and catastrophic forgetting in FCIL is a critical and complex challenge, and the proposed two-pronged approach (GDR and TTS) offers a comprehensive solution, making it a strong contribution to the general machine learning community targeted by ICML.
why_it_does_not_fit: Reviewer A noted that the practical computational overhead of SVD 'could still be a consideration in extremely large-scale FL scenarios', which hints at potential scalability limitations that might be a concern for ICML if the problem size were significantly larger than tested.

why_it_fits: The paper directly addresses 'General machine learning: core contributions in supervised and unsupervised methods' by tackling Federated Class-Incremental Learning, a fundamental challenge in dynamic machine learning environments.

The methods proposed, particularly the Federated Learning aspect with privacy-preserving SVD ('AI and network science' and 'Data-centric aspects of AI'), and the incremental learning aspect ('Generalization and multi-task learning'), align perfectly with NeurIPS identified topics.

why_it_does_not_fit: While the paper's topic is relevant, ICLR places a very strong emphasis on novel deep learning architectures, theoretical advancements directly related to deep learning, or significant applications of deep learning. This paper's primary focus is Federated Class-Incremental Learning, which, while using deep learning, is not solely about architectural innovation or foundational deep learning theory, but more about strategy leveraging existing models.

strengths: The core idea of integrating global-perspective data replay (GDR) with task-aware temperature scaling (TTS) to address both inter-client and inter-task class imbalance in FCIL is highly novel and innovative. The use of SVD for privacy-preserving global feature aggregation is particularly clever.

The performance improvements across diverse datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet), varying heterogeneity levels, and different task splits are consistently strong, showing significant gains over state-of-the-art baselines. The comparison to LANDER, which uses a large generative model, highlights the efficiency of this approach.

The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the individual and synergistic contributions of the GDR and TTS modules, providing strong empirical support for the proposed architecture. The visualization of per-class sample distributions and attention maps further reinforces the qualitative impact of FedCBDR.
weaknesses: While the paper emphasizes privacy-preserving aspects of SVD, the actual security guarantees and privacy leakage risks associated with reconstructing global representations from client-encrypted features could be discussed in greater detail. The current treatment feels a bit high-level for a mechanism specifically designed for privacy-preservation.

The sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters for TTS (ω_old, ω_new, τ_old, τ_new) suggests that precise tuning is crucial for optimal performance. This could be a practical limitation in real-world FCIL deployments where hyperparameter tuning across many clients and tasks can be prohibitive.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative and bold approach to Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL) by tackling the critical issues of class imbalance and catastrophic forgetting. The dual-mechanism of Global-perspective Data Replay (GDR) for balanced sampling and Task-aware Temperature Scaling (TTS) for loss re-weighting is highly creative. The use of SVD to aggregate global features in a privacy-preserving manner is a clever technical contribution that pushes the boundaries of what is possible in FL. While some minor concerns exist regarding the depth of privacy analysis and hyperparameter sensitivity, these do not detract from the overall novelty and significant potential impact of the work. The extensive experimental validation, showing consistent and substantial improvements over SOTA methods, firmly supports the claims. This paper introduces genuinely new ideas that could inspire substantial future research in FCIL, making it a strong candidate for acceptance.

strengths: The paper rigorously addresses a critical problem in Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL): class imbalance in replay buffers and between historical and new tasks. The proposed FedCBDR method provides a well-reasoned two-pronged approach to tackle these issues.

The methodology is clearly articulated, with the Global-perspective Data Replay (GDR) module using a pseudo-global representation via SVD for importance-driven sampling, and the Task-aware Temperature Scaling (TTS) module dynamically adjusting loss objectives. The use of SVD for privacy-preserving feature aggregation is a clever and sound approach.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive and thorough. It spans three datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) across various heterogeneity levels (Dirichlet β), different task splits, and comparisons against six state-of-the-art methods. The ablation studies, analysis of replay buffer size, local training epochs, and per-task performance, along with visualizations (Grad-CAM, per-class sample distributions), provide strong evidence for the effectiveness and robustness of FedCBDR.

The quantitative results demonstrate significant performance gains (2%-15% Top-1 accuracy improvement) over baselines, especially under challenging non-IID and high-task-split scenarios. The consistent superior performance across diverse settings highlights the practical utility of the proposed method.
weaknesses: While the concept of using SVD for pseudo-feature construction is presented, the mathematical details of `Inverse SVD` in Equation (1) are rather unusual and potentially confusing. Specifically, `X_k^{(i)'} = P_k^{(i)} X_k^{(i)} Q^{(i)}` where `P_k^{(i)}` is `|D_k^{(i)}| x |D_k^{(i)}|` and `Q^{(i)}` is `d x d`, while `X_k^{(i)}` is `|D_k^{(i)}| x d` creates a dimension mismatch unless `P_k^{(i)}` is implied to be a transformation matrix for rows and `Q^{(i)}` for columns. A more precise mathematical definition of this 'Inverse SVD' operation is needed to ensure full clarity and soundness.

The hyperparameter tuning of `τ_old`, `τ_new`, `ω_old`, and `ω_new` for the TTS module seems crucial, as indicated by the sensitivity analysis. While the paper states they are selected within certain ranges, the exact procedure for choosing these optimal values (e.g., cross-validation on a held-out set, grid search) is not explicitly detailed. This could impact the reproducibility of the results and the effort required to apply FedCBDR to new tasks.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents FedCBDR, a well-conceived method for Federated Class-Incremental Learning that addresses class imbalance through global-perspective data replay and task-aware temperature scaling. The proposed techniques are sound in principle, and the extensive experimental validation across multiple datasets and heterogeneous settings convincingly demonstrates the superior performance and robustness of FedCBDR over existing state-of-the-art methods. Despite a minor ambiguity in the mathematical definition of 'Inverse SVD' and the lack of explicit detail on hyperparameter tuning, the overall methodological rigor and strong empirical results make this a significant contribution to the field. The detailed ablation studies and sensitivity analyses further strengthen the paper's claims. I recommend acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and practical problem in Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL): class imbalance in replay buffers and between replayed and new tasks. This is a common challenge in real-world FL deployments, and finding effective solutions has tangible benefits.

The proposed FedCBDR method, with its Global-Perspective Data Replay (GDR) and Task-Aware Temperature Scaling (TTS) modules, is a well-thought-out approach. The use of SVD for privacy-preserving global representation and leverage scores for importance-driven sampling is a clever way to achieve global awareness without compromising data privacy. The TTS module directly tackles the inherent class imbalance between prior and current tasks, which is a crucial aspect for practical application.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive and convincing. It includes comparisons against six state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets and heterogeneity levels, thorough ablation studies, analysis of buffer size, and detailed per-class distribution comparisons. The reported performance gains (2%-15% Top-1 accuracy) are substantial and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of FedCBDR.
weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges the computational cost of SVD and provides some analysis in the appendix, a more explicit and detailed discussion on the practical overhead of the client-side ISVD and server-side SVD, especially for very large models or numerous clients, would be beneficial for practitioners. While the authors state the cost is "relatively small," quantifying this more rigorously or discussing trade-offs would be valuable.

The sensitivity analysis of the temperature and sample weighting hyperparameters (Figure 4) indicates that inappropriate choices can harm performance. While the paper finds optimal settings for its experiments, a more robust hyperparameter tuning strategy or a method to adaptively determine these parameters in a Federated Learning setting (where data distributions can shift) would enhance the practical applicability and reduce the operational burden for users.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents FedCBDR, a novel and practically relevant approach to Federated Class-Incremental Learning. It addresses the critical issues of class imbalance and catastrophic forgetting through two well-designed modules: Global-Perspective Data Replay for balanced exemplar selection and Task-Aware Temperature Scaling for dynamic loss reweighting. The method demonstrates strong performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art techniques across various settings, backed by extensive and thorough experimental validation. The focus on privacy-preserving global coordination and mitigating inherent data imbalances makes this work highly significant for real-world FL deployments. While some practical considerations regarding computational overhead and hyperparameter robustness could be further elaborated, the overall contribution is solid and impactful.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel and unified framework for understanding neural network symmetries, going beyond traditional permutations to include semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and general invertible maps. This is a significant conceptual advancement.

For the first time, this work demonstrates low- and zero-loss linear mode connectivity (LMC) in Transformers (Vision Transformers and GPT-2), which was previously thought to be notoriously difficult. This result challenges existing assumptions about the Transformer loss landscape and opens new avenues for research.

The proposed 'learned matching' method, particularly when leveraging the broader symmetry classes, effectively achieves near-zero barriers for LMC, showcasing the practical utility of the theoretical framework.
weaknesses: While the concept of generalized symmetries is bold, some mathematical details, especially around 'semi-permutations' and their practical application for alignment, could be more rigorously defined or illustrated with clearer examples beyond just piecewise-linear functions.

The evaluation on language models, particularly GPT-2, was performed on smaller versions due to resource constraints. This limits the generalizability of the findings to larger, state-of-the-art Transformer models, which are a major focus of current research.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly exciting and novel perspective on linear mode connectivity in neural networks, particularly for Transformers. The core idea of generalizing symmetry classes beyond simple permutations to include semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and invertible maps is a significant conceptual leap. The empirical demonstration of zero-loss LMC in Vision Transformers and GPT-2 for the first time is a groundbreaking result that will undoubtedly inspire further research in understanding the geometry of neural network loss landscapes and re-parameterization techniques. While there are minor points regarding the depth of mathematical rigor for some new concepts and the constrained evaluation on large LMs, these do not overshadow the bold and impactful contribution of this work. The paper pushes the field forward substantially and opens up many interesting future directions, aligning perfectly with my preference for innovative and forward-thinking research. I strongly recommend acceptance.

strengths: The core idea of expanding symmetry classes beyond permutations (to include semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and general invertible maps) is highly novel and significantly pushes the boundaries of understanding neural network loss landscapes, especially for Transformers. This is a crucial advancement for LMC research.

The paper achieves a breakthrough by demonstrating linear mode connectivity in complex, modern architectures like Vision Transformers and GPT-2, which previous permutation-only approaches failed to do. This empirical validation of the extended symmetry framework is compelling.
The framework's ability to handle multi-model connectivity and width-heterogeneous alignment is a forward-looking contribution, opening avenues for more robust model merging and ensemble techniques.

The distinction between weight matching and learned matching, and the analysis of where the performance gap lies (primarily in the orthogonal map for the residual stream), provides valuable practical insights and future research directions.
weaknesses: While the theoretical formalization of the symmetry classes is presented, the mathematical rigor in Appendix E still feels a bit informal in its connection to the overall functional equivalence, especially for the broader invertible maps. More concrete proofs or a deeper dive into the exact conditions under which these transformations strictly preserve functionality would strengthen the soundness. The reparameterization of RMSNorm, while interesting, still leaves some questions about full functional equivalence under all stated transformations.

The evaluation, while impressive, relies on smaller versions of GPT-2 and standard benchmarks for ViTs. target_paper_summary.title: Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity For Transformers
target_paper_summary.abstract: Understanding the geometry of neural network loss landscapes is a central question in deep learning, with implications for generalization and optimization. A striking phenomenon is *linear mode connectivity* (LMC), where independently trained models can be connected by low- or zero-barrier paths, despite appearing to lie in separate loss basins. However, this is often obscured by symmetries in parameter space—such as neuron permutations—which make functionally equivalent models appear dissimilar. Prior work has predominantly focused on neuron reordering through permutations, but such approaches are limited in scope and fail to capture the richer symmetries exhibited by modern architectures such as Transformers. In this work, we introduce a unified framework that captures four symmetry classes—permutations, semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and general invertible maps—broadening the set of valid reparameterizations and subsuming many previous approaches as special cases. Crucially, this generalization enables, for the first time, the discovery of low- and zero-barrier linear interpolation paths between independently trained Vision Transformers and GPT-2 models. Furthermore, our framework extends beyond pairwise alignment, to multi-model and width-heterogeneous settings, enabling alignment across architectures of different sizes. These results reveal deeper structure in the loss landscape and underscore the importance of symmetry-aware analysis for understanding model space geometry. Our code is available here.

paper_metadata.title: Putting the ‘landscape’ in landscape genetics
Resting-State Functional Connectivity Emerges from Structurally and Dynamically Shaped Slow Linear Fluctuations
paper_metadata.abstract: Brain fluctuations at rest are not random but are structured in spatial patterns of correlated activity across different brain areas. The question of how resting-state functional connectivity (FC) emerges from the brain's anatomical connections has motivated several experimental and computational studies to understand structure-function relationships. However, the mechanistic origin of resting state is obscured by large-scale models' complexity, and a close structure-function relation is still an open problem. Thus, a realistic but simple enough description of relevant brain dynamics is needed. Here, we derived a dynamic mean field model that consistently summarizes the realistic dynamics of a detailed spiking and conductance-based synaptic large-scale network, in which connectivity is constrained by diffusion imaging data from human subjects. The dynamic mean field approximates the ensemble dynamics, whose temporal evolution is dominated by the longest time scale of the system. With this reduction, we demonstrated that FC emerges as structured linear fluctuations around a stable low firing activity state close to destabilization. Moreover, the model can be further and crucially simplified into a set of motion equations for statistical moments, providing a direct analytical link between anatomical structure, neural network dynamics, and FC. Our study suggests that FC arises from noise propagation and dynamical slowing down of fluctuations in an anatomically constrained dynamical system. Altogether, the reduction from spiking models to statistical moments presented here provides a new framework to explicitly understand the building up of FC through neuronal dynamics underpinned by anatomical connections and to drive hypotheses in task-evoked studies and for clinical applications.

paper_metadata.title: The Deep Arbitrary Polynomial Chaos Neural Network or how Deep Artificial Neural Networks could benefit from Data-Driven Homogeneous Chaos Theory
paper_metadata.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Machine learning have been widely used in various fields of mathematical computing, physical modeling, computational science, communication science, and stochastic analysis. Approaches based on Deep Artificial Neural Networks (DANN) are very popular in our days. Depending on the learning task, the exact form of DANNs is determined via their multi-layer architecture, activation functions and the so-called loss function. However, for a majority of deep learning approaches based on DANNs, the kernel structure of neural signal processing remains the same, where the node response is encoded as a linear superposition of neural activity, while the non-linearity is triggered by the activation functions. In the current paper, we suggest to analyze the neural signal processing in DANNs from the point of view of homogeneous chaos theory as known from polynomial chaos expansion (PCE). From the PCE perspective, the (linear) response on each node of a DANN could be seen as a $1^{st}$ degree multi-variate polynomial of single neurons from the previous layer, i.e. linear weighted sum of monomials. From this point of view, the conventional DANN structure relies implicitly (but erroneously) on a Gaussian distribution of neural signals. Additionally, this view revels that by design DANNs do not necessarily fulfill any orthogonality or orthonormality condition for a majority of data-driven applications. Therefore, the prevailing handling of neural signals in DANNs could lead to redundant representation as any neural signal could contain some partial information from other neural signals. To tackle that challenge, we suggest to employ the data-driven generalization of PCE theory known as arbitrary polynomial chaos (aPC) to construct a corresponding multi-variate orthonormal representations on each node of a DANN to obtain Deep arbitrary polynomial chaos neural networks.

paper_metadata.title: Percolation Approach to Study Connectivity in Living Neural Networks
paper_metadata.abstract: We study neural connectivity in cultures of rat hippocampal neurons. We measure the neurons' response to an electric stimulation for gradual lower connectivity, and characterize the size of the giant cluster in the network. The connectivity undergoes a percolation transition described by the critical exponent $β\simeq 0.65$. We use a theoretic approach based on bond.percolation on a graph to describe the process of disintegration of the network and extract its statistical properties.
