target_paper_summary.title: Elasticmm: Efficient Multimodal Llms Serving With Elastic Multimodal Parallelism
target_paper_summary.abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend LLMs to handle images, videos, and audio by incorporating feature extractors and projection modules. However, these additional components—combined with complex inference pipelines and heterogeneous workloads—introduce significant inference overhead. Therefore, efficiently serving MLLMs remains a major challenge. Current tightly coupled serving architectures struggle to distinguish between mixed request types or adapt parallelism strategies to different inference stages, leading to increased time-to-first-token (TTFT) and poor resource utilization. To address this, we introduce Elastic Multimodal Parallelism (EMP), a new serving paradigm that elastically adapts to resource heterogeneity across request types and inference stages. Building upon EMP, we develop ElasticMM, an MLLM serving system that
(1) separates requests into independent modality groups with dynamic resource allocation via a modality-aware load balancer; (2) decouples inference stages and enables parallelism adjustment and adaptive scaling via elastic partition scheduling; and (3) improves inference efficiency through unified multimodal prefix caching and non-blocking encoding. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets show that ElasticMM outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) serving systems, reducing TTFT by up to 4.2× and achieving 3.2–4.5× higher throughput while meeting service-level objectives (SLOs).

paper_metadata.title: A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models
paper_metadata.abstract: Recently, Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) represented by GPT-4V has been a new rising research hotspot, which uses powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) as a brain to perform multimodal tasks. The surprising emergent capabilities of MLLM, such as writing stories based on images and OCR-free math reasoning, are rare in traditional multimodal methods, suggesting a potential path to artificial general intelligence. To this end, both academia and industry have endeavored to develop MLLMs that can compete with or even better than GPT-4V, pushing the limit of research at a surprising speed. In this paper, we aim to trace and summarize the recent progress of MLLMs. First of all, we present the basic formulation of MLLM and delineate its related concepts, including architecture, training strategy and data, as well as evaluation. Then, we introduce research topics about how MLLMs can be extended to support more granularity, modalities, languages, and scenarios. We continue with multimodal hallucination and extended techniques, including Multimodal ICL (M-ICL), Multimodal CoT (M-CoT), and LLM-Aided Visual Reasoning (LAVR). To conclude the paper, we discuss existing challenges and point out promising research directions. In light of the fact that the era of MLLM has only just begun, we will keep updating this survey and hope it can inspire more research. An associated GitHub link collecting the latest papers is available at https://github.com/BradyFU/Awesome-Multimodal-Large-Language-Models.

paper_metadata.title: MLLM-DataEngine: An Iterative Refinement Approach for MLLM
paper_metadata.abstract: Despite the great advance of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in both instruction dataset building and benchmarking, the independence of training and evaluation makes current MLLMs hard to further improve their capability under the guidance of evaluation results with a relatively low human cost. In this paper, we propose MLLM-DataEngine, a novel closed-loop system that bridges data generation, model training, and evaluation. Within each loop iteration, the MLLM-DataEngine first analyze the weakness of the model based on the evaluation results, then generate a proper incremental dataset for the next training iteration and enhance the model capability iteratively. Compared with previous data collection methods which are separate from the benchmarking, the data generated by MLLM-DataEngine shows better targeting, quality, and correctness. For targeting, we propose an Adaptive Bad-case Sampling module, which adjusts the ratio of different types of data within each incremental dataset based on the benchmarking results. For quality, we resort to GPT-4 to generate high-quality data with each given data type. For correctness, prompt design is critical for the data generation results. Rather than previous hand-crafted prompt, we propose an Interactive Prompt Optimization strategy, which optimizes the prompt with the multi-round interaction between human and GPT, and improve the correctness of generated data greatly. Through extensive experiments, we find our MLLM-DataEngine could boost the MLLM capability in a targeted and automatic manner, with only a few human participation. We hope it could be a general solution for the following MLLMs building. The MLLM-DataEngine has been open-sourced and is now available at https://github.com/opendatalab/MLLM-DataEngine.

paper_metadata.title: A Realistic Simulation Testbed of A Turbocharged Spark-Ignited Engine System: A Platform for the Evaluation of Fault Diagnosis Algorithms and Strategies
paper_metadata.abstract: Research on fault diagnosis on highly nonlinear dynamic systems such as the engine of a vehicle have garnered huge interest in recent years, especially with the automotive industry heading towards self-driving technologies. This article presents a novel opensource simulation testbed of a turbocharged spark ignited (TCSI) petrol engine system for testing and evaluation of residuals generation and fault diagnosis methods. Designed and developed using Matlab/Simulink, the user interacts with the testbed using a GUI interface, where the engine can be realistically simulated using industrial-standard driving cycles such as the Worldwide harmonized Light vehicles Test Procedures (WLTP), the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC), the Extra-Urban Driving Cycle (EUDC), and EPA Federal Test Procedure (FTP-75). The engine is modeled using the mean value engine model (MVEM) and is controlled using a proportional-integral (PI)-based boost controller. The GUI interface also allows the user to induce one of the 11 faults of interest, so that their effects on the performance of the engine are better understood. This minimizes the risk of causing permanent damages to the engine and shortening its lifespan, should the tests be conducted onto the actual physical system. This simulation testbed will serve 16 as an excellent platform where researchers can generate critical data to develop and compare current and future research methods for fault diagnosis of automotive engine systems.

paper_metadata.title: A Dynamic-System-Based Approach to Modeling Driver Movements Across General-Purpose/Managed Lane Interfaces
paper_metadata.abstract: To help mitigate road congestion caused by the unrelenting growth of traffic demand, many transportation authorities have implemented managed lane policies, which restrict certain freeway lanes to certain types of vehicles. It was originally thought that managed lanes would improve the use of existing infrastructure through demand-management behaviors like carpooling, but implementations have often been characterized by unpredicted phenomena that are sometimes detrimental to system performance. The development of traffic models that can capture these sorts of behaviors is a key step for helping managed lanes deliver on their promised gains. Towards this goal, this paper presents an approach for solving for driver behavior of entering and exiting managed lanes at the macroscopic (i.e., fluid approximation of traffic) scale. Our method is inspired by recent work in extending a dynamic-system-based modeling framework from traffic behaviors on individual roads, to models at junctions, and can be considered a further extension of this dynamic-system paradigm to the route/lane choice problem. Unlike traditional route choice models that are often based on discrete-choice methods and often rely on computing and comparing drivers' estimated travel times from taking different routes, our method is agnostic to the particular choice of physical traffic model and is suited specifically towards making decisions at these interfaces using only local information. These features make it a natural drop-in component to extend existing dynamic traffic modeling methods.

paper_metadata.title: Parallel Batch-Dynamic Graph Connectivity
paper_metadata.abstract: In this paper, we study batch parallel algorithms for the dynamic connectivity problem, a fundamental problem that has received considerable attention in the sequential setting. The most well known sequential algorithm for dynamic connectivity is the elegant level-set algorithm of Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup (HDT), which achieves $O(\log^2 n)$ amortized time per edge insertion or deletion, and $O(\log n / \log\log n)$ time per query. We design a parallel batch-dynamic connectivity algorithm that is work-efficient with respect to the HDT algorithm for small batch sizes, and is asymptotically faster when the average batch size is sufficiently large. Given a sequence of batched updates, where $Δ$ is the average batch size of all deletions, our algorithm achieves $O(\log n \log(1 + n / Δ))$ expected amortized work per edge insertion and deletion and $O(\log^3 n)$ depth w.h.p. Our algorithm answers a batch of $k$ connectivity queries in $O(k \log(1 + n/k))$ expected work and $O(\log n)$ depth w.h.p. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm is the first parallel batch-dynamic algorithm for connectivity.

rag_package.related_work_summary: Efficiently serving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is a significant challenge due to their complex architectures and heterogeneous workloads. Prior work has explored various aspects of MLLMs, with surveys such as A Survey on Multimodal Large Language Models (Yin et al., 2023) outlining their architectures, training, and evaluation, thereby establishing the foundation and importance of this field. While the core challenge of MLLM serving efficiency is distinct, general concepts of dynamic parallelism and adaptive resource allocation have been explored in other domains, for example, Parallel Batch-Dynamic Graph Connectivity (Acar et al., 2019) which discusses parallel batch-dynamic algorithms for graph operations, and to a lesser extent, A Dynamic-System-Based Approach to Modeling Driver Movements Across General-Purpose/Managed Lane Interfaces (Wright et al., 2018), which models dynamic systems for resource management in traffic. Efforts like MLLM-DataEngine: An Iterative Refinement Approach for MLLM (Zhao et al., 2023) focus on improving MLLM capabilities through iterative refinement and benchmarking of model performance. However, these works do not directly address the unique challenges of efficiently serving diverse, real-world MLLM workloads while meeting service-level objectives.

4.desc: No RAG, 3 iterations, 1 reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The core idea of 'Elastic Multimodal Parallelism' (EMP) with its two-level hierarchical scheduling (modality-aware load balancing and elastic partitioned scheduling) is genuinely novel and addresses a critical problem in MLLM serving. This is a significant conceptual leap over existing tightly coupled or statically disaggregated systems.

The paper provides a comprehensive and compelling analysis of the limitations of existing MLLM serving systems, clearly motivating the need for a decoupled and elastic approach. The key insights are well-articulated, making the problem space very clear.

The proposed multimodal inference optimizations (Unified Multimodal Prefix Cache and Non-blocking Encoding) are clever and practical additions that directly tackle MLLM-specific overheads without compromising model accuracy, which is a major advantage over accuracy-trading methods found in related work.
weaknesses: While the paper claims to meet SLOs, the evaluation plots (Figure 5) show 'Normalized Latency' rather than raw latency against QPS. Although the authors clarified that throughput is measured under strict SLO adherence, making this more explicit in the main results (e.g., by plotting raw latency against QPS with an SLO boundary, or including a small plot in the appendix as suggested) would further strengthen the evaluation's clarity for direct comparison.

The 'gain-cost model' for elastic scaling (Equations 2 and 3) is presented, but a more in-depth discussion of the tunable penalty factor 'w' and how it is determined or tuned would be beneficial. While the authors explained it's empirically derived, elaborating on the range of 'w', how its value affects the system's behavior (e.g., responsiveness vs. stability), and practical guidelines for its calibration beyond 'offline profiling' would enhance the paper.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a highly novel and significant approach to efficiently serving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The core concept of Elastic Multimodal Parallelism (EMP), which introduces both modality-aware load balancing and elastic partitioned scheduling, is a creative and forward-thinking solution to the challenges posed by heterogeneous MLLM workloads. The idea of decoupling inference stages and dynamically allocating resources at different granularities is a substantial advancement over the current state-of-the-art. The empirical results, demonstrating significant improvements in TTFT and throughput, are very encouraging. The authors have adequately addressed my concerns regarding the clarity of SLO achievements and the 'w' factor by committing to further explanations and additional plots in the revised manuscript. These clarifications will significantly improve the presentation. This paper introduces an exciting new paradigm that will undoubtedly inspire future research in MLLM serving. paper_metadata.title: Byzantine-Resilient SGD in High Dimensions on Heterogeneous Data
paper_metadata.abstract: We study distributed stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the master-worker architecture under Byzantine attacks. We consider the heterogeneous data model, where different workers may have different local datasets, and we do not make any probabilistic assumptions on data generation. At the core of our algorithm, we use the polynomial-time outlier-filtering procedure for robust mean estimation proposed by Steinhardt et al. (ITCS 2018) to filter-out corrupt gradients. In order to be able to apply their filtering procedure in our {\em heterogeneous} data setting where workers compute {\em stochastic} gradients, we derive a new matrix concentration result, which may be of independent interest. We provide convergence analyses for smooth strongly-convex and non-convex objectives. We derive our results under the bounded variance assumption on local stochastic gradients and a {\em deterministic} condition on datasets, namely, gradient dissimilarity; and for both these quantities, we provide concrete bounds in the statistical heterogeneous data model. We give a trade-off between the mini-batch size for stochastic gradients and the approximation error. Our algorithm can tolerate up to $\frac{1}{4}$ fraction Byzantine workers. It can find approximate optimal parameters in the strongly-convex setting exponentially fast and reach to an approximate stationary point in the non-convex setting with a linear speed, thus, matching the convergence rates of vanilla SGD in the Byzantine-free setting. We also propose and analyze a Byzantine-resilient SGD algorithm with gradient compression, where workers send $k$ random coordinates of their gradients. Under mild conditions, we show a $\frac{d}{k}$-factor saving in communication bits as well as decoding complexity over our compression-free algorithm without affecting its convergence rate (order-wise) and the approximation error.

paper_metadata.title: Data Encoding for Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Optimization
paper_metadata.abstract: We study distributed optimization in the presence of Byzantine adversaries, where both data and computation are distributed among $m$ worker machines, $t$ of which may be corrupt. The compromised nodes may collaboratively and arbitrarily deviate from their pre-specified programs, and a designated (master) node iteratively computes the model/parameter vector for generalized linear models. In this work, we primarily focus on two iterative algorithms: Proximal Gradient Descent (PGD) and Coordinate Descent (CD). Gradient descent (GD) is a special case of these algorithms. PGD is typically used in the data-parallel setting, where data is partitioned across different samples, whereas, CD is used in the model-parallelism setting, where data is partitioned across the parameter space. In this paper, we propose a method based on data encoding and error correction over real numbers to combat adversarial attacks. We can tolerate up to $t\leq \lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\rfloor$ corrupt worker nodes, which is information-theoretically optimal. We give deterministic guarantees, and our method does not assume any probability distribution on the data. We develop a {\em sparse} encoding scheme which enables computationally efficient data encoding and decoding. We demonstrate a trade-off between the corruption threshold and the resource requirements (storage, computational, and communication complexity). As an example, for $t\leq\frac{m}{3}$, our scheme incurs only a {\em constant} overhead on these resources, over that required by the plain distributed PGD/CD algorithms which provide no adversarial protection. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first paper that makes CD secure against adversarial attacks. Our encoding scheme extends efficiently to the data streaming model and for stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We also give experimental results to show the efficacy of our proposed schemes.

paper_metadata.title: AeroGen: Enhancing Remote Sensing Object Detection with Diffusion-Driven Data Generation
paper_metadata.abstract: Remote sensing image object detection (RSIOD) aims to identify and locate specific objects within satellite or aerial imagery. However, there is a scarcity of labeled data in current RSIOD datasets, which significantly limits the performance of current detection algorithms. Although existing techniques, e.g., data augmentation and semi-supervised learning, can mitigate this scarcity issue to some extent, they are heavily dependent on high-quality labeled data and perform worse in rare object classes. To address this issue, this paper proposes a layout-controllable diffusion generative model (i.e. AeroGen) tailored for RSIOD. To our knowledge, AeroGen is the first model to simultaneously support horizontal and rotated bounding box condition generation, thus enabling the generation of high-quality synthetic images that meet specific layout and object category requirements. Additionally, we propose an end-to-end data augmentation framework that integrates a diversity-conditioned generator and a filtering mechanism to enhance both the diversity and quality of generated data. Experimental results demonstrate that the synthetic data produced by our method are of high quality and diversity. Furthermore, the synthetic RSIOD data can significantly improve the detection performance of existing RSIOD models, i.e., the mAP metrics on DIOR, DIOR-R, and HRSC datasets are improved by 3.7%, 4.3%, and 2.43%, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/Sonettoo/AeroGen.

paper_metadata.title: Changing Data Sources in the Age of Machine Learning for Official Statistics
paper_metadata.abstract: Data science has become increasingly essential for the production of official statistics, as it enables the automated collection, processing, and analysis of large amounts of data. With such data science practices in place, it enables more timely, more insightful and more flexible reporting. However, the quality and integrity of data-science-driven statistics rely on the accuracy and reliability of the data sources and the machine learning techniques that support them. In particular, changes in data sources are inevitable to occur and pose significant risks that are crucial to address in the context of machine learning for official statistics. This paper gives an overview of the main risks, liabilities, and uncertainties associated with changing data sources in the context of machine learning for official statistics. We provide a checklist of the most prevalent origins and causes of changing data sources; not only on a technical level but also regarding ownership, ethics, regulation, and public perception. Next, we highlight the repercussions of changing data sources on statistical reporting. These include technical effects such as concept drift, bias, availability, validity, accuracy and completeness, but also the neutrality and potential discontinuation of the statistical offering. We offer a few important precautionary measures, such as enhancing robustness in both data sourcing and statistical techniques, and thorough monitoring. In doing so, machine learning-based official statistics can maintain integrity, reliability, consistency, and relevance in policy-making, decision-making, and public discourse.

paper_metadata.title: DOME: Recommendations for supervised machine learning validation in biology
authors: The ELIXIR Machine Learning focus group
paper_metadata.abstract: Modern biology frequently relies on machine learning to provide predictions and improve decision processes. There have been recent calls for more scrutiny on machine learning performance and possible limitations. Here we present a set of community-wide recommendations aiming to help establish standards of supervised machine learning validation in biology. Adopting a structured methods description for machine learning based on data, optimization, model, evaluation (DOME) will aim to help both reviewers and readers to better understand and assess the performance and limitations of a method or outcome. The recommendations are formulated as questions to anyone wishing to pursue implementation of a machine learning algorithm. Answers to these questions can be easily included in the supplementary material of published papers.

paper_metadata.title: Towards Corruption-Agnostic Robust Domain Adaptation
paper_metadata.abstract: Big progress has been achieved in domain adaptation in decades. Existing works are always based on an ideal assumption that testing target domain are i.i.d. with training target domains. However, due to unpredictable corruptions (e.g., noise and blur) in real data like web images, domain adaptation methods are increasingly required to be corruption robust on target domains. In this paper, we investigate a new task, Corruption-agnostic Robust Domain Adaptation (CRDA): to be accurate on original data and robust against unavailable-for-training corruptions on target domains. This task is non-trivial due to large domain discrepancy and unsupervised target domains. We observe that simple combinations of popular methods of domain adaptation and corruption robustness have sub-optimal CRDA results. We propose a new approach based on two technical insights into CRDA: 1) an easy-to-plug module called Domain Discrepancy Generator (DDG) that generates samples that enlarge domain discrepancy to mimic unpredictable corruptions; 2) a simple but effective teacher-student scheme with contrastive loss to enhance the constraints on target domains. Experiments verify that DDG keeps or even improves performance on original data and achieves better corruption robustness that baselines.

paper_metadata.title: Robust Core-Periphery Constrained Transformer for Domain Adaptation
paper_metadata.abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to learn transferable representation across domains. Recently a few UDA works have successfully applied Transformer-based methods and achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. However, it remains challenging when there exists a large domain gap between the source and target domain. Inspired by humans' exceptional transferability abilities to adapt knowledge from familiar to uncharted domains, we try to apply the universally existing organizational structure in the human functional brain networks, i.e., the core-periphery principle to design the Transformer and improve its UDA performance. In this paper, we propose a novel brain-inspired robust core-periphery constrained transformer (RCCT) for unsupervised domain adaptation, which brings a large margin of performance improvement on various datasets. Specifically, in RCCT, the self-attention operation across image patches is rescheduled by an adaptively learned weighted graph with the Core-Periphery structure (CP graph), where the information communication and exchange between images patches are manipulated and controlled by the connection strength, i.e., edge weight of the learned weighted CP graph. Besides, since the data in domain adaptation tasks can be noisy, to improve the model robustness, we intentionally add perturbations to the patches in the latent space to ensure generating robust learned weighted core-periphery graphs. Extensive evaluations are conducted on several widely tested UDA benchmarks. Our proposed RCCT consistently performs best compared to existing works, including 88.3\% on Office-Home, 95.0\% on Office-31, 90.7\% on VisDA-2017, and 46.0\% on DomainNet.

strengths: The core idea that a *positive distribution shift* can improve test performance is highly novel and challenges a fundamental, often implicit, assumption in machine learning. This is a bold and exciting premise.

The paper provides a theoretical framework to systematically analyze this phenomenon across various learning models (orthogonal power law, memorization tasks, transfer learning), demonstrating that optimal training proportions often deviate from test proportions.

The 'almost always better to mismatch' argument in Section 7, backed by formal proofs, is a powerful and thought-provoking contribution, suggesting that this isn't just a niche phenomenon but a general principle.
weaknesses: While the theoretical analysis is robust, the experimental evaluation is quite limited, with only one synthetic task on skill composition mentioned. More empirical validation on real-world datasets across different learning scenarios would significantly strengthen the paper's claims.

Some of the theoretical derivations, particularly in Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.3, are quite dense and could benefit from more detailed intuition or clearer step-by-step explanations for readers not deeply familiar with the mathematical notation.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly novel and potentially field-shifting idea: that mismatching training and test distributions can actually improve performance. This directly challenges a foundational assumption in ML research. The theoretical framework is comprehensive, exploring several relevant learning models and culminating in a compelling argument that this 'positive distribution shift' is a general rule rather than an exception. While the experimental validation is somewhat minimal, the conceptual novelty and the strength of the theoretical arguments make this a highly significant contribution. Minor technical imperfections are acceptable given the groundbreaking nature of the core idea. This work has the potential to inspire a new direction in how we think about data collection and training strategies. No rebuttal was provided, so my review remains unchanged.

paper_metadata.title: Improving Gradient Computation for Differentiable Physics Simulation with Contacts
paper_metadata.abstract: Differentiable simulation enables gradients to be back-propagated through physics simulations. In this way, one can learn the dynamics and properties of a physics system by gradient-based optimization or embed the whole differentiable simulation as a layer in a deep learning model for downstream tasks, such as planning and control. However, differentiable simulation at its current stage is not perfect and might provide wrong gradients that deteriorate its performance in learning tasks. In this paper, we study differentiable rigid-body simulation with contacts. We find that existing differentiable simulation methods provide inaccurate gradients when the contact normal direction is not fixed - a general situation when the contacts are between two moving objects. We propose to improve gradient computation by continuous collision detection and leverage the time-of-impact (TOI) to calculate the post-collision velocities. We demonstrate our proposed method, referred to as TOI-Velocity, on two optimal control problems. We show that with TOI-Velocity, we are able to learn an optimal control sequence that matches the analytical solution, while without TOI-Velocity, existing differentiable simulation methods fail to do so.

paper_metadata.title: Capturing Dependencies within Machine Learning via a Formal Process Model
paper_metadata.abstract: The development of Machine Learning (ML) models is more than just a special case of software development (SD): ML models acquire properties and fulfill requirements even without direct human interaction in a seemingly uncontrollable manner. Nonetheless, the underlying processes can be described in a formal way. We define a comprehensive SD process model for ML that encompasses most tasks and artifacts described in the literature in a consistent way. In addition to the production of the necessary artifacts, we also focus on generating and validating fitting descriptions in the form of specifications. We stress the importance of further evolving the ML model throughout its life-cycle even after initial training and testing. Thus, we provide various interaction points with standard SD processes in which ML often is an encapsulated task. Further, our SD process model allows to formulate ML as a (meta-) optimization problem. If automated rigorously, it can be used to realize self-adaptive autonomous systems. Finally, our SD process model features a description of time that allows to reason about the progress within ML development processes. This might lead to further applications of formal methods within the field of ML.

paper_metadata.title: On the Complexity of Computing Minimal Unsatisfiable LTL formulas
paper_metadata.abstract: We show that (1) the Minimal False QCNF search-problem (MF-search) and the Minimal Unsatisfiable LTL formula search problem (MU-search) are FPSPACE complete because of the very expressive power of QBF/LTL, (2) we extend the PSPACE-hardness of the MF decision problem to the MU decision problem. As a consequence, we deduce a positive answer to the open question of PSPACE hardness of the inherent Vacuity Checking problem. We even show that the Inherent Non Vacuous formula search problem is also FPSPACE-complete.

paper_metadata.title: A Neutral Temporal Deontic STIT Logic
paper_metadata.abstract: In this work we answer a long standing request for temporal embeddings of deontic STIT logics by introducing the multi-agent STIT logic TDS. The logic is based upon atemporal utilitarian STIT logic. Yet, the logic presented here will be neutral: instead of committing ourselves to utilitarian theories, we prove the logic TDS sound and complete with respect to relational frames not employing any utilitarian function. We demonstrate how these neutral frames can be transformed into utilitarian temporal frames, while preserving validity. Last, we discuss problems that arise from employing binary utility functions in a temporal setting.

paper_metadata.title: Propositional computability logic I
paper_metadata.abstract: In the same sense as classical logic is a formal theory of truth, the recently initiated approach called computability logic is a formal theory of computability. It understands (interactive) computational problems as games played by a machine against the environment, their computability as existence of a machine that always wins the game, logical operators as operations on computational problems, and validity of a logical formula as being a scheme of "always computable" problems. The present contribution gives a detailed exposition of a soundness and completeness proof for an axiomatization of one of the most basic fragments of computability logic. The logical vocabulary of this fragment contains operators for the so called parallel and choice operations, and its atoms represent elementary problems, i.e. predicates in the standard sense. This article is self-contained as it explains all relevant concepts. While not technically necessary, however, familiarity with the foundational paper "Introduction to computability logic" [Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 123 (2003), pp.1-99] would greatly help the reader in understanding the philosophy, underlying motivations, potential and utility of computability logic, -- the context that determines the value of the present results. Online introduction to the subject is available at http://www.cis.upenn.edu/~giorgi/cl.html and http://www.csc.villanova.edu/~japaridz/CL/gsoll.html .

rag_package.related_work_summary: Ensuring learned controllers comply with safety and reliability requirements in real-world reinforcement learning settings remains a significant challenge. While formal specification languages like Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) offer a robust way to derive correct-by-construction learning objectives, their inherent sparse rewards often hinder efficient learning. Existing work such as "Improving Gradient Computation for Differentiable Physics Simulation with Contacts" by Zhong et al. (2023) has focused on refining differentiable simulation itself, tackling issues like inaccurate gradient computation under varying contact conditions, which is foundational to gradient-based learning. Other efforts, like "Capturing Dependencies within Machine Learning via a Formal Process Model" by Ritz et al. (2022), explore formal process models for machine learning and emphasize proper specification. However, a unified approach that effectively integrates LTL with differentiable simulators for efficient gradient-based learning while mitigating the sparse-reward problem without compromising objective correctness has been lacking. Our work addresses this gap by proposing the first method, to our knowledge, that accelerates learning from LTL specifications using differentiable simulators, demonstrating significant improvements in reward attainment and training time compared to discrete methods.

4.desc: No RAG, 3 iterations, 1 reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The core idea of combining LTL with differentiable simulators to address sparse reward issues is highly novel and represents a significant conceptual leap for formal methods in RL.

The introduction of 'soft labeling' for differentiable rewards and states in LTL automata is an elegant solution to a critical problem, enabling gradient-based optimization in a traditionally discrete domain.

The empirical results clearly demonstrate that the proposed differentiable LTL approach significantly outperforms non-differentiable baselines, especially in complex, higher-dimensional scenarios, opening up new possibilities for robust and verifiable robotic control.
weaknesses: The reliance on specific differentiable simulators and their quality/efficiency can limit generalizability or introduce new bottlenecks. While acknowledged by the authors, a deeper analysis of this dependency, perhaps examining performance sensitivity to simulator quality, would further strengthen the work.

The 'soft labeling' technique introduces an additional hyperparameter (the CDF function like sigmoid) which needs tuning. While the authors state it performed well in their experiments and its robustness to minor variations, a more thorough exploration of its impact and robustness to different choices, or adaptive tuning strategies, could be a valuable addition for future work.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative approach to integrating formal methods, specifically Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), with deep reinforcement learning. The central idea of leveraging differentiable simulators to make LTL rewards and automaton transitions differentiable is a bold and forward-thinking concept that addresses the long-standing challenge of sparse rewards in LTL-guided RL. The 'soft labeling' technique is a clever mechanism to achieve this differentiability without sacrificing the correctness of the LTL specification. The authors have adequately addressed the identified weaknesses by further elaborating on their points and clarifying their perspectives. They correctly reiterate that the reliance on simulator quality is inherent to any differentiable simulation method and that their current approach leverages state-of-the-art tools while being generalizable. They also confirm that the chosen sigmoid function for soft labeling was effective for establishing the foundational methodology, acknowledging that further exploration of other functions or tuning is a valid direction for future research. These responses are reasonable and do not diminish the strong novelty and significance of the presented work. The results are compelling, showing clear performance gains over traditional non-differentiable methods on challenging robotic tasks. This work has strong potential to inspire a new wave of research at the intersection of formal methods and differentiable programming, pushing the field of safe and verifiable AI forward.

why_it_fits: The paper introduces a novel method for accelerating learning in Reinforcement Learning (RL) using Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications and differentiable simulators, which directly aligns with ICML's interest in 'general machine learning' (reinforcement learning section) and 'optimization' (stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) by leveraging gradient-based methods.

The core contribution of integrating LTL with differentiable simulators for gradient-based learning to address sparse rewards is a significant methodological advancement in RL, a topic prominently featured at ICML. The use of 'soft labeling' for differentiable rewards and states is a clever technical innovation.

The paper provides strong empirical validation on robotic tasks (CartPole, Hopper, Cheetah, Ant) demonstrating considerable performance improvements over state-of-the-art non-differentiable baselines. This aligns with ICML's emphasis on empirical evidence for novel machine learning techniques.

The paper discusses the theoretical underpinnings (product MDPs, LDBAs) and provides intuitive explanations, supported by references to complete proofs, which fits ICML's attention to theoretical rigor in machine learning research. As Reviewer A notes, it's a 'significant conceptual leap for formal methods in RL'.
why_it_does_not_fit: While the paper demonstrates strong empirical results, the 'reliance on hyper-parameters' and the 'additional hyperparameter' for the CDF function (as noted in the weaknesses and acknowledged by Reviewer A) hint at aspects that might require more extensive meta-studies or sensitivity analyses that are sometimes expected for broad applicability in ICML.

Reviewer A mentioned that a 'deeper analysis of this dependency' on simulator quality and 'more thorough exploration of its impact and robustness to different choices' for soft labeling could strengthen the work, indicating areas where the rigor could be further expanded for a top-tier ML conference, particularly at the intersection of ML and robotics.

why_it_fits: The paper's focus on Reinforcement Learning for robotic control, ensuring safety and reliability with formal specifications (LTL), is a strong fit for NeurIPS, which has dedicated topics like 'Decision-making, reinforcement learning, and control' and 'Robotics, embodied systems, and engineering'.

The novel approach of using differentiable simulators to overcome sparse rewards in LTL-guided RL, particularly with the introduction of 'soft labeling', presents an 'original research' contribution that NeurIPS highly values, especially those that bridge interdisciplinary areas as this paper does (formal methods, RL, differentiable simulation).

The empirical demonstrations on robotic platforms (CartPole, various legged robots) clearly show 'significant improvements in both reward attainment and training time' and support the claims. This practical application of ML to robotics makes it relevant to NeurIPS's applied ML interests.

The paper effectively addresses a key challenge in deploying AI systems in real-world scenarios – ensuring controllers comply with safety and reliability requirements, a topic that aligns with NeurIPS's general interest in 'socio-technical aspects of AI' and robust AI systems.
why_it_does_not_fit: While strong, the paper's primary novelty centers on the integration of LTL via differentiable simulation, which is a niche area. While NeurIPS welcomes interdisciplinary work, the deep theoretical underpinnings of LTL and formal methods might be more specialized than some of the broader machine learning topics prioritized by some NeurIPS reviewers.

The reviewer's comments about the dependency on simulator quality and the tuning of the CDF function (hyperparameter) could be perceived as limitations in the robustness or generalization of the approach. For a broad conference like NeurIPS, a more exhaustive analysis of these factors could further strengthen the work's appeal across diverse sub-communities.

The 'Others' classification for the paper topic suggests it might not perfectly align with one of the mainstream, high-volumeNeurIPS categories, potentially leading to reviewer assignment challenges, though the specific themes of RL and Robotics are strong pointers.

why_it_fits: ICLR explicitly focuses on 'deep learning' and related areas, including 'reinforcement learning', 'optimization', and 'applications to robotics, autonomy, planning'. This paper's core contribution, accelerating RL with LTL using differentiable simulation, is highly relevant.

The paper's emphasis on differentiable programming (using PyTorch, dFlex) to enable gradient-based learning in a previously discrete domain (LTL rewards and automaton transitions) strongly aligns with ICLR's interest in 'infrastructure, software libraries, hardware, etc.' and advancements in differentiable approaches.

The innovative 'soft labeling' technique, which makes LTL rewards and automaton states differentiable, is a methodological contribution squarely within the realm of representation learning and generative models, areas of significant interest at ICLR because it enables differentiable operations where only discrete ones existed previously.

The empirical success in complex robotic environments (CartPole, Hopper, Cheetah, Ant) demonstrates practical application of novel deep learning techniques in a relevant domain, aligning with ICLR's focus on applications to robotics and real-world systems.
why_it_does_not_fit: While the paper uses deep RL baselines, the fundamental novelty lies in making formal logic (LTL) compatible with differentiable simulation. Some ICLR submissions are more directly focused on novel neural network architectures or core deep learning algorithms, which is not the primary focus here.

The problem's framing, while addressing a critical safety aspect, heavily relies on formal methods and automata theory, which might be a step removed from the typical deep learning audience, potentially requiring more background explanation for a general ICLR reviewer than for someone specialized in formal methods in RL.

The limitations regarding 'reliance on hyperparameters' and the tunable CDF function (as highlighted by Reviewer A) suggest that while the core idea is strong, the practical deployability and hyperparameter sensitivity might need further robust analysis for a deep learning audience looking for readily applicable methods.

strengths: The core idea of leveraging differentiable simulators to enable gradient-based learning directly from LTL specifications is highly novel and addresses a critical limitation in LTL-based RL, which traditionally suffers from sparse rewards. This pushes the boundaries of combining formal methods with modern RL techniques.

The introduction of 'soft labeling' and probabilistic ε-actions to ensure differentiability of LTL rewards and automaton transitions is a clever and innovative technical contribution that directly tackles the main challenge of integrating LTL with differentiable RL.

The paper demonstrates significant practical improvements in learning speed and reward attainment across various robotic tasks (CartPole, Hopper, Cheetah, Ant) compared to established non-differentiable RL baselines. This provides strong empirical evidence for the utility and impact of the proposed method.
weaknesses: While the concept of 'soft labeling' and probabilistic transitions is well-explained, the specific choice of the sigmoid function as the differentiable CDF is mentioned as being replaceable by 'any differentiable CDF'. However, the paper does not explore the sensitivity of the results to this choice, which could potentially impact performance or the smoothness of the gradients.

The reliance on various hyperparameters, including the CDF choice and those inherited from the differentiable simulators and RL algorithms (as acknowledged in the discussion), suggests that the method might require substantial tuning for new environments or more complex LTL specifications. Further analysis or guidance on hyperparameter selection would strengthen the generalizability.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative approach to accelerate reinforcement learning with Linear Temporal Logic specifications by integrating it with differentiable simulators. The novel idea of 'soft labeling' to achieve differentiable rewards and automaton transitions is a significant technical leap, allowing for gradient-based optimization in a domain previously plagued by sparse, discrete rewards. The empirical results clearly demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in terms of learning speed and reward attainment across diverse robotic control tasks. While there are some minor concerns regarding the sensitivity to the choice of differentiable CDF and hyperparameter tuning, these do not undermine the bold and forward-thinking nature of this research. This work has the potential to inspire substantial future work at the intersection of formal methods and differentiable RL, making it a strong candidate for acceptance.

strengths: The paper rigorously develops a differentiable framework for incorporating LTL specifications into reinforcement learning, addressing the critical issues of sparse rewards and non-differentiability inherent in traditional LTL-based RL approaches.

The proposed 'soft labeling' technique for probabilistic AP satisfaction and automaton transitions is well-formulated and provides a clear mechanism for achieving differentiability while maintaining the logical correctness of LTL specifications.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, comparing the proposed differentiable LTL approach with both non-differentiable (PPO, SAC) and differentiable (SHAC, AHAC) RL baselines across multiple robotic environments, clearly demonstrating the performance benefits in terms of reward attainment and learning speed. The ablation study further strengthens these claims.
weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges that the choice of CDF for probability estimation is a hyperparameter to be tuned, specific guidance or an analysis of its sensitivity/impact on different LTL formulas and environments would be beneficial (e.g., how the sigmoid function affects gradient landscape).

The paper mentions that 'All assumptions are explicitly formalized for each theoretical statement' in the NeurIPS checklist, but only cites existing proofs for Lemma 1 and Theorem 1. Explicitly detailing the assumptions and providing the full derivations for the differentiable transition functions (fL, fε, f) or rewards/discounting (R, D) in the main text or appendix would enhance the completeness and self-containment of the theoretical presentation for the proposed differentiable components.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a strong contribution to the field of safe and formally verifiable reinforcement learning. The core idea of integrating LTL specifications with differentiable simulators through 'soft labeling' to overcome sparse and discrete rewards is both novel and methodologically sound. The paper's technical development of differentiable probabilistic APs, automaton transitions, rewards, and discounting functions is well-explained and appears logically consistent. The extensive experimental validation across various robotic tasks, demonstrating significant improvements over both differentiable and non-differentiable baselines, provides convincing evidence of the method's efficacy. The ablation study further reinforces the paper's central claims. Although some minor improvements could be made regarding the detailed theoretical derivations of the proposed differentiable components and hyperparameter guidance, these do not overshadow the overall rigor and impact of the work. The paper is clearly written and provides sufficient details for understanding and potential reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant practical bottleneck in safe reinforcement learning: the challenge of sparse rewards when using formal methods like LTL. By integrating differentiable simulators and soft labeling, the authors offer a compelling solution for accelerating learning while maintaining correctness.

The experimental evaluation is thorough and convincing. The comparison against both non-differentiable and differentiable RL baselines, across multiple robotic environments (CartPole, Hopper, Cheetah, Ant), clearly demonstrates the practical advantages of the proposed method in terms of both maximium return achieved and learning speed.

The introduction of 'soft labeling' for LTL automaton transitions is a clever and well-justified technical contribution. This approach successfully bridges the gap between discrete logical specifications and the continuous, gradient-based optimization required by differentiable simulators, making the entire pipeline end-to-end differentiable.
weaknesses: While the paper acknowledges the reliance on hyperparameter tuning and the quality of differentiable simulators as limitations, it could benefit from a more in-depth discussion or examples of how these factors specifically influence practical deployment or robustness in real-world scenarios. For instance, is the "soft labeling" sensitive to the choice of the CDF or its parameters?

The paper briefly mentions that for non-differentiable baselines, there was no performance difference between differentiable and discrete LTL rewards. A short explanation or hypothesis for this observation would be valuable, as it further underscores why the proposed 'soft labeling' is critical for differentiable methods and not a general fix for sparse LTL rewards in non-differentiable settings.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a strong and practically relevant contribution to the field of safe reinforcement learning. The core idea of combining Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) with differentiable simulators through 'soft labeling' to overcome sparse reward issues is innovative and well-executed. The problem is clearly motivated, and the proposed solution directly addresses a major challenge in deploying formally-verified controllers. The experimental results provide compelling evidence of the method's effectiveness across various robotic tasks, demonstrating significant improvements over existing baselines. The paper is well-written and easy to understand, making the complex technical details accessible. While acknowledging the limitations of its reliance on underlying differentiable simulators and hyperparameter tuning, the work provides a solid foundation for more robust and efficient learning of LTL-specified policies.

why_it_fits: The paper directly addresses 'general machine learning' issues by tackling sparse rewards in RL, a fundamental learning challenge, aligning with topics like 'active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis'.

The use of Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) for safety and reliability requirements in RL places it squarely within 'trustworthy machine learning' topics such as 'reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety'.

The integration of differentiable simulators for gradient-based learning aligns with 'machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.)' and 'optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.)'.

The application to robotic systems (CartPole, Hopper, Cheetah, Ant) fits 'application-driven machine learning' as it introduces innovative techniques relevant to robotic control within the ML community.

Reviewers consistently highlight the 'highly novel' and 'innovative approach' (Reviewer A) of leveraging differentiable simulators for LTL, and the 'clever and innovative technical contribution' (Reviewer A) of soft labeling, which aligns with ICML's focus on cutting-edge research.

The rigorous experimental evaluation demonstrating 'significant improvements in both reward attainment and training time' (Abstract, Reviewer A, B, C) provides strong empirical backing valued by ICML.
why_it_does_not_fit: While LTL falls under theoretical computer science, the paper primarily emphasizes the practical application and empirical performance in RL, rather than deep theoretical analysis or foundational machine learning theory. why_it_fits: The paper's core topic of 'Reinforcement learning' is explicitly listed under NeurIPS's topics, and specifically 'Decision-making, reinforcement learning, and control'.

why_it_fits: The paper's focus on 'reinforcement learning' is a key topic for ICLR, as highlighted in its introduction and topic list.

The method uses 'differentiable simulators' and 'gradient-based learning' to accelerate RL, which aligns with ICLR's strong emphasis on 'optimization' and 'large-scale learning and non-convex optimization'.

The experimental success using 'PyTorch-based differentiable physics simulator dFlex' and various deep RL algorithms (SHAC, AHAC, PPO, SAC) showcases concrete implementations of 'infrastructure, software libraries, hardware, etc.', and supports ICLR's practical, deep learning-focused content.
why_it_does_not_fit: While LTL is connected to formal methods, the paper does not delve deeply into 'learning theory' or 'causal reasoning' from a purely theoretical perspective. Its primary contribution is methodological and empirical, rather than theoretical guarantees specifically for deep learning architectures.

The paper does not explicitly discuss or propose novel deep learning 'architectures' or 'generative models', which are often central to ICLR submissions, though it leverages existing deep RL algorithms.

Reviewers mentioned the sensitivity to hyperparameter choices (Reviewer A, C), which, given ICLR's strong focus on robust and generalizable deep learning methods, could be a point of minor contention if not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: The core idea of reformulating de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) as a continuous mass prediction problem to enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs is highly novel and represents a significant conceptual leap forward for the field.

The use of multi-task learning with a combination of experimental and simulated spectra is a creative approach to bridge the domain gap and facilitate generalization, showing a clear forward-thinking strategy.

The paper provides a compelling proof-of-concept for mass-based representations as a path towards truly open-search DNPS, which has the potential to unlock the discovery of novel biological insights related to PTMs.
weaknesses: While the concept is strong, the current experimental evaluation shows limited practical generalization to unseen PTMs on experimental data (e.g., recall rates for methionine oxidation and cysteine carbamidomethylation remain low), indicating that a significant performance gap still needs to be addressed for real-world application.

The use of teacher forcing during evaluation, while understandable for isolating individual residue prediction ability, means the results do not fully reflect the real-world, autoregressive performance of the model where error accumulation could be a major challenge.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative and conceptually bold approach to de novo peptide sequencing by reframing it as a continuous mass prediction task. This shift is crucial for addressing the long-standing limitation of fixed vocabularies in existing DNPS models, paving the way for zero-shot discovery of novel PTMs. While the current experimental results on unseen PTMs are still somewhat limited and the use of teacher forcing hides some practical challenges, the fundamental idea of mass-based zero-shot learning is highly significant and opens up entirely new research avenues. The authors acknowledge the limitations, positioning this as a proof-of-concept, which is fair given the exploratory nature of such a disruptive idea. I believe this work strongly pushes the field forward and deserves acceptance for its novelty and potential impact.

why_it_fits: The paper introduces a novel deep learning-based approach (transformer-based mass prediction with GAN-inspired multi-task learning) for de novo peptide sequencing, which aligns well with ICML's strong interest in 'deep learning architectures' and 'general machine learning' for 'application-driven machine learning' in areas like 'computational biology' and 'healthcare'.

The core contribution is a methodological advancement in machine learning (reformulating DNPS as a mass prediction problem for zero-shot learning) to address a significant limitation in proteomics, fitting ICML's focus on 'innovative techniques' and 'problems of interest to the machine learning community'.

The use of multi-task learning and adversarial training for generalization aligns with ICML's interest in 'trustworthy machine learning' (e.g., reliability, causality) and 'optimization' and 'generative models'.
Reviewer A highlights the 'highly novel' core idea and 'significant conceptual leap,' aligning with ICML's emphasis on cutting-edge research and advancing the field.
why_it_does_not_fit: While the application is clear, the primary focus is on a specific biological problem (de novo peptide sequencing for PTMs), which might be perceived as niche compared to more general machine learning advancements often prioritized at ICML, though 'application-driven machine learning' is a topic.

The experimental evaluation, as noted by Reviewer A, shows 'limited practical generalization to unseen PTMs on experimental data' and relies on 'teacher forcing' during evaluation, suggesting that the empirical results, while promising as a 'proof-of-concept,' are not yet fully production-ready, which might be a slight drawback for a conference that also values strong practical demonstrations.

why_it_fits: The paper introduces a novel machine learning method (mass-based zero-shot learning for DNPS using transformers and MTL) directly applicable to 'AI/ML for health and biotechnology', which is a specific topic of interest for NeurIPS.

The approach, leveraging deep learning (transformer-based architecture) and probabilistic methods (implicitly through continuous mass prediction and error estimation), fits well within the general machine learning and deep learning topics covered by NeurIPS.

The focus on addressing the 'zero-shot' prediction of unseen post-translational modifications speaks to NeurIPS's interest in 'generalization and multi-task learning' and 'data-centric aspects of AI' (handling diverse and sparse data like PTMs).

Reviewer A acknowledges the 'innovative and conceptually bold approach' and its potential for 'new research avenues', which aligns with NeurIPS's emphasis on interdisciplinary and groundbreaking research.
why_it_does_not_fit: Similar to ICML, while biology/health applications are explicitly listed, the highly specialized nature of 'de novo peptide sequencing' might still place it slightly outside the very broadest core ML audience at NeurIPS compared to more foundational or widely applicable ML advances.

Reviewer A's concern about the 'limited practical generalization' and reliance on 'teacher forcing' for evaluation points to the current stage of the work as a 'proof-of-concept' rather than a fully robust, generalizable system. NeurIPS often favors strong empirical results or theoretical guarantees alongside novel methods, and the empirical gaps here, while acknowledged, could be a hurdle.

The paper does not involve significant theoretical results or an in-depth analysis of existing methods' limitations beyond the 'fixed vocabulary' problem, which are sometimes highlighted in NeurIPS's call for papers.

why_it_fits: The paper is explicitly 'transformer-based' and uses 'deep learning' for 'representation learning' (mass-based representations), directly aligning with ICLR's primary focus on deep learning architectures and methods.

The concept of 'zero-shot learning' and 'multi-task learning' for generalization to unseen data aligns with ICLR's interest in 'transfer learning, meta learning, and lifelong learning' and 'representation learning'.
The use of 'adversarial multi-task learning scheme' relates to 'generative models' and 'optimization' themes at ICLR.
The application to 'computational biology' (de novo peptide sequencing) is listed as an 'important application area' for ICLR, solidifying the topic fit.
Reviewer A praises the 'novelty' and 'conceptual leap,' which is highly valued at ICLR, especially in terms of new architectures and learning paradigms.
why_it_does_not_fit: While deep learning is central, the paper describes the work as a 'proof-of-concept' with current limitations in 'practical generalization to unseen PTMs on experimental data,' which may fall short of the strong empirical results often expected at ICLR for deep learning applications.

The reliance on 'teacher forcing' for evaluation, as highlighted by Reviewer A, indicates that the model's performance in a fully autoregressive, real-world setting with error accumulation is not comprehensively demonstrated, which could be a significant concern for ICLR reviewers valuing robust empirical validation for deep learning models.
The paper's evaluation, while clear, might lack the extensive benchmarking against state-of-the-art deep learning models in the domain that ICLR often looks for, given its deep learning focus.

strengths: The core idea of reformulating de novo peptide sequencing as a continuous mass prediction problem to enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs is highly novel and addresses a critical limitation in current models. This is a genuinely bold and forward-thinking approach.

The paper introduces an innovative multi-task learning strategy that combines experimental and simulated spectra with a GAN-inspired adversarial component. This creative blend of techniques is well-motivated to tackle the generalization challenge.

The work has high potential significance for the field of proteomics. True open-search de novo sequencing could revolutionize the discovery of novel PTMs and peptides from unsequenced organisms, pushing the boundaries of what's currently possible.
weaknesses: While the concept is strong, the current experimental results show limited practical generalization to truly novel modifications on experimental data. The recall for unseen PTMs remains low (e.g., 3.18% for C[Carbamidomethylation]), indicating significant room for improvement before it becomes a production-ready system.

The evaluation is primarily in 'teacher-forcing' mode, which isolates residue-level prediction but bypasses the full autoregressive decoding challenge. This makes it difficult to assess the overall end-to-end performance and error accumulation in a more realistic setting.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents an incredibly novel and ambitious approach to de novo peptide sequencing by reframing the problem as continuous mass prediction. This zero-shot learning strategy for unseen PTMs is exactly the kind of forward-thinking research that can genuinely advance the field, even if it's currently a proof-of-concept. While the practical performance on unseen PTMs in experimental data isn't yet stellar, the core idea is groundbreaking and the multi-task learning with adversarial components is an innovative step in the right direction. Minor methodological imperfections in initial performance are acceptable given the immense potential impact and novelty of the approach. This work lays a crucial foundation for future research in open-search proteomics.

why_it_fits: The paper introduces a novel machine learning approach (re-framing DNPS as a mass prediction problem with zero-shot learning) for a complex and important application area (computational biology/proteomics), which aligns well with ICML's interest in 'application-driven machine learning' and 'general machine learning' with innovative techniques.
The use of transformer-based architectures, multi-task learning, and GAN-inspired adversarial components falls under 'deep learning' and 'optimization' topics, which are core to ICML's scope.

The paper provides a 'proof of concept' for an innovative machine learning methodology, which ICML often values for its potential to open new research directions, even if not yet fully production-ready, as noted by 'Reviewer A: Minor methodological imperfections in initial performance are acceptable given the immense potential impact and novelty of the approach.'
ICML welcomes papers that introduce innovative techniques within established machine learning paradigms, and the adversarial multi-task learning scheme fits this criterion.
why_it_does_not_fit: While the topic is application-driven, the current experimental results, particularly the low recall for unseen PTMs (e.g., 3.18%), might be seen as less quantitatively robust than some ICML papers, affecting the 'Contribution Fit' and 'Rigor Fit' to some extent.

The evaluation being primarily in 'teacher-forcing' mode, as highlighted by Reviewer A, indicates that the full end-to-end performance in a more realistic setting has not been thoroughly demonstrated, which could be a concern for 'Rigor Fit' in a competitive venue like ICML.

why_it_fits: The paper's focus on 'AI/ML for health and biotechnology' and its application to proteomics aligns directly with NeurIPS's explicitly stated topics.

The use of transformer-based models, multi-task learning, and probabilistic methods (mass prediction can be viewed probabilistically in error margins) fits within NeurIPS's general machine learning and deep learning interests.

NeurIPS encourages 'interdisciplinary submissions that do not fit neatly into existing categories' and 'in-depth analysis of existing methods that provide new insights in terms of their limitations or behavior beyond the scope of the original work.' This paper's reformulation of DNPS and exploration of zero-shot learning addresses significant limitations of current models.
The 'highly novel and addresses a critical limitation' nature of the work ('Reviewer A') is a strong fit for NeurIPS, which highly values groundbreaking research.
why_it_does_not_fit: Similar to ICML, the current 'limited practical generalization to truly novel modifications on experimental data' and the low recall for unseen PTMs might raise questions about the practical impact and 'Rigor Fit' at NeurIPS.

The evaluation mostly in 'teacher-forcing' mode, as mentioned by Reviewer A, could be perceived as not fully demonstrating the model's performance in a real-world, end-to-end scenario, potentially impacting 'Rigor Fit' for a conference that also values strong empirical validation.

target_paper_summary.title: Towards Open-Search De Novo Peptide Sequencing Via Mass-Based Zero-Shot Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Proteins are the main drivers of biochemical processes and play a pivotal role in 2 almost all cellular functions. Through post-translational modifications (PTMs), 3 residues within a protein can be chemically modified to fine-tune the protein's 4 function in the cellular context. Despite the importance of PTMs, the plethora 5 of deep learning-based de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) models, which, in 6 contrast to database searching approaches, predict peptide sequence solely from 7 tandem mass spectra without any reference organism database, can only predict 8 peptide sequences with a limited set of PTMs. This is because they rely on fixed 9 vocabularies that map residue tokens to non-generalizable learned embeddings. To 10 overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning. Specifically, we reformulate DNPS as a 13 mass prediction problem instead of a multiclass classification problem, where the 14 model predicts the mass of the next residue instead of its token representation. To 15 facilitate generalization to unseen PTMs, we leverage an adversarial multi-task 16 learning scheme by supplementing the training data of experimental spectra with 17 simulated spectra that mimic spectra containing unseen residues. We show that our 18 approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising 19 proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search 20 DNPS.

paper_metadata.title: Transformer-based de novo peptide sequencing for data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry
paper_metadata.abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) stands as the predominant high-throughput technique for comprehensively analyzing protein content within biological samples. This methodology is a cornerstone driving the advancement of proteomics. In recent years, substantial strides have been made in Data-Independent Acquisition (DIA) strategies, facilitating impartial and non-targeted fragmentation of precursor ions. The DIA-generated MS/MS spectra present a formidable obstacle due to their inherent high multiplexing nature. Each spectrum encapsulates fragmented product ions originating from multiple precursor peptides. This intricacy poses a particularly acute challenge in de novo peptide/protein sequencing, where current methods are ill-equipped to address the multiplexing conundrum. In this paper, we introduce DiaTrans, a deep-learning model based on transformer architecture. It deciphers peptide sequences from DIA mass spectrometry data. Our results show significant improvements over existing STOA methods, including DeepNovo-DIA and PepNet. Casanovo-DIA enhances precision by 15.14% to 34.8%, recall by 11.62% to 31.94% at the amino acid level, and boosts precision by 59% to 81.36% at the peptide level. Integrating DIA data and our DiaTrans model holds considerable promise to uncover novel peptides and more comprehensive profiling of biological samples. Casanovo-DIA is freely available under the GNU GPL license at https://github.com/Biocomputing-Research-Group/DiaTrans.

paper_metadata.title: ContraNovo: A Contrastive Learning Approach to Enhance De Novo Peptide Sequencing
paper_metadata.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing from mass spectrometry (MS) data is a critical task in proteomics research. Traditional de novo algorithms have encountered a bottleneck in accuracy due to the inherent complexity of proteomics data. While deep learning-based methods have shown progress, they reduce the problem to a translation task, potentially overlooking critical nuances between spectra and peptides. In our research, we present ContraNovo, a pioneering algorithm that leverages contrastive learning to extract the relationship between spectra and peptides and incorporates the mass information into peptide decoding, aiming to address these intricacies more efficiently. Through rigorous evaluations on two benchmark datasets, ContraNovo consistently outshines contemporary state-of-the-art solutions, underscoring its promising potential in enhancing de novo peptide sequencing. The source code is available at https://github.com/BEAM-Labs/ContraNovo.

paper_metadata.title: DePS: An improved deep learning model for de novo peptide sequencing
paper_metadata.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing from mass spectrometry data is an important method for protein identification. Recently, various deep learning approaches were applied for de novo peptide sequencing and DeepNovoV2 is one of the represetative models. In this study, we proposed an enhanced model, DePS, which can improve the accuracy of de novo peptide sequencing even with missing signal peaks or large number of noisy peaks in tandem mass spectrometry data. It is showed that, for the same test set of DeepNovoV2, the DePS model achieved excellent results of 74.22%, 74.21% and 41.68% for amino acid recall, amino acid precision and peptide recall respectively. Furthermore, the results suggested that DePS outperforms DeepNovoV2 on the cross species dataset.

paper_metadata.title: New views of old proteins: clarifying the enigmatic proteome
authors: Participants in a NIH Workshop on Functional
paper_metadata.abstract: All human diseases involve proteins, yet our current tools to characterize and quantify them are limited. To better elucidate proteins across space, time, and molecular composition, we provide provocative projections for technologies to meet the challenges that protein biology presents. With a broad perspective, we discuss grand opportunities to transition the science of proteomics into a more propulsive enterprise. Extrapolating recent trends, we offer potential futures for a next generation of disruptive approaches to define, quantify and visualize the multiple dimensions of the proteome, thereby transforming our understanding and interactions with human disease in the coming decade.

More robust metrics tied to chemical accuracy and discrete assignment are needed for PTM prediction.

For instance, comparing the MTL model's performance on 'seen' PTMs with a baseline classification-based model (like Casanovo) on the *same test set* would provide a clearer picture of the trade-offs introduced by the mass-based approach and MTL for common PTMs.
