paper_metadata.title: The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: We describe the new field of mathematical analysis of deep learning. This field emerged around a list of research questions that were not answered within the classical framework of learning theory. These questions concern: the outstanding generalization power of overparametrized neural networks, the role of depth in deep architectures, the apparent absence of the curse of dimensionality, the surprisingly successful optimization performance despite the non-convexity of the problem, understanding what features are learned, why deep architectures perform exceptionally well in physical problems, and which fine aspects of an architecture affect the behavior of a learning task in which way. We present an overview of modern approaches that yield partial answers to these questions. For selected approaches, we describe the main ideas in more detail.

paper_metadata.title: Sparse Coding: A Deep Learning using Unlabeled Data for High - Level Representation
paper_metadata.abstract: Sparse coding algorithm is an learning algorithm mainly for unsupervised feature for finding succinct, a little above high - level Representation of inputs, and it has successfully given a way for Deep learning. Our objective is to use High - Level Representation data in form of unlabeled category to help unsupervised learning task. when compared with labeled data, unlabeled data is easier to acquire because, unlike labeled data it does not follow some particular class labels. This really makes the Deep learning wider and applicable to practical problems and learning. The main problem with sparse coding is it uses Quadratic loss function and Gaussian noise mode. So, its performs is very poor when binary or integer value or other Non- Gaussian type data is applied. Thus first we propose an algorithm for solving the L1 - regularized convex optimization algorithm for the problem to allow High - Level Representation of unlabeled data. Through this we derive a optimal solution for describing an approach to Deep learning algorithm by using sparse code.

paper_metadata.title: The Deep Arbitrary Polynomial Chaos Neural Network or how Deep Artificial Neural Networks could benefit from Data-Driven Homogeneous Chaos Theory
paper_metadata.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Machine learning have been widely used in various fields of mathematical computing, physical modeling, computational science, communication science, and stochastic analysis. Approaches based on Deep Artificial Neural Networks (DANN) are very popular in our days. Depending on the learning task, the exact form of DANNs is determined via their multi-layer architecture, activation functions and the so-called loss function. However, for a majority of deep learning approaches based on DANNs, the kernel structure of neural signal processing remains the same, where the node response is encoded as a linear superposition of neural activity, while the non-linearity is triggered by the activation functions. In the current paper, we suggest to analyze the neural signal processing in DANNs from the point of view of homogeneous chaos theory as known from polynomial chaos expansion (PCE). From the PCE perspective, the (linear) response on each node of a DANN could be seen as a $1^{st}$ degree multi-variate polynomial of single neurons from the previous layer, i.e. linear weighted sum of monomials. From this point of view, the conventional DANN structure relies implicitly (but erroneously) on a Gaussian distribution of neural signals. Additionally, this view revels that by design DANNs do not necessarily fulfill any orthogonality or orthonormality condition for a majority of data-driven applications. Therefore, the prevailing handling of neural signals in DANNs could lead to redundant representation as any neural signal could contain some partial information from other neural signals. To tackle that challenge, we suggest to employ the data-driven generalization of PCE theory known as arbitrary polynomial chaos (aPC) to construct a corresponding multi-variate orthonormal representations on each node of a DANN to obtain Deep arbitrary polynomial chaos neural networks.

paper_metadata.title: Improving Generalization of Deep Neural Networks by Leveraging Margin Distribution
paper_metadata.abstract: Recent research has used margin theory to analyze the generalization performance for deep neural networks (DNNs). The existed results are almost based on the spectrally-normalized minimum margin. However, optimizing the minimum margin ignores a mass of information about the entire margin distribution, which is crucial to generalization performance. In this paper, we prove a generalization upper bound dominated by the statistics of the entire margin distribution. Compared with the minimum margin bounds, our bound highlights an important measure for controlling the complexity, which is the ratio of the margin standard deviation to the expected margin. We utilize a convex margin distribution loss function on the deep neural networks to validate our theoretical results by optimizing the margin ratio. Experiments and visualizations confirm the effectiveness of our approach and the correlation between generalization gap and margin ratio.

paper_metadata.title: SelfMatch: Combining Contrastive Self-Supervision and Consistency for Semi-Supervised Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: This paper introduces SelfMatch, a semi-supervised learning method that combines the power of contrastive self-supervised learning and consistency regularization. SelfMatch consists of two stages: (1) self-supervised pre-training based on contrastive learning and (2) semi-supervised fine-tuning based on augmentation consistency regularization. We empirically demonstrate that SelfMatch achieves the state-of-the-art results on standard benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10 and SVHN. For example, for CIFAR-10 with 40 labeled examples, SelfMatch achieves 93.19% accuracy that outperforms the strong previous methods such as MixMatch (52.46%), UDA (70.95%), ReMixMatch (80.9%), and FixMatch (86.19%). We note that SelfMatch can close the gap between supervised learning (95.87%) and semi-supervised learning (93.19%) by using only a few labels for each class.

paper_metadata.title: Towards Label-efficient Automatic Diagnosis and Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey of Advanced Deep Learning-based Weakly-supervised, Semi-supervised and Self-supervised Techniques in Histopathological Image Analysis
paper_metadata.abstract: Histopathological images contain abundant phenotypic information and pathological patterns, which are the gold standards for disease diagnosis and essential for the prediction of patient prognosis and treatment outcome. In recent years, computer-automated analysis techniques for histopathological images have been urgently required in clinical practice, and deep learning methods represented by convolutional neural networks have gradually become the mainstream in the field of digital pathology. However, obtaining large numbers of fine-grained annotated data in this field is a very expensive and difficult task, which hinders the further development of traditional supervised algorithms based on large numbers of annotated data. More recent studies have started to liberate from the traditional supervised paradigm, and the most representative ones are the studies on weakly supervised learning paradigm based on weak annotation, semi-supervised learning paradigm based on limited annotation, and self-supervised learning paradigm based on pathological image representation learning. These new methods have led a new wave of automatic pathological image diagnosis and analysis targeted at annotation efficiency. With a survey of over 130 papers, we present a comprehensive and systematic review of the latest studies on weakly supervised learning, semi-supervised learning, and self-supervised learning in the field of computational pathology from both technical and methodological perspectives. Finally, we present the key challenges and future trends for these techniques.

paper_metadata.title: Learn to Accumulate Evidence from All Training Samples: Theory and Practice
paper_metadata.abstract: Evidential deep learning, built upon belief theory and subjective logic, offers a principled and computationally efficient way to turn a deterministic neural network uncertainty-aware. The resultant evidential models can quantify fine-grained uncertainty using the learned evidence. To ensure theoretically sound evidential models, the evidence needs to be non-negative, which requires special activation functions for model training and inference. This constraint often leads to inferior predictive performance compared to standard softmax models, making it challenging to extend them to many large-scale datasets. To unveil the real cause of this undesired behavior, we theoretically investigate evidential models and identify a fundamental limitation that explains the inferior performance: existing evidential activation functions create zero evidence regions, which prevent the model to learn from training samples falling into such regions. A deeper analysis of evidential activation functions based on our theoretical underpinning inspires the design of a novel regularizer that effectively alleviates this fundamental limitation. Extensive experiments over many challenging real-world datasets and settings confirm our theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

rag_package.related_work_summary: Estimating the generalization gap and developing optimization techniques for improved performance on unseen data are critical challenges in deep learning. Alternative generalization measures and optimization strategies are actively explored. This includes approaches that improve generalization by leveraging the margin distribution (Lyu et al., 2018). Furthermore, the ability to exploit unlabeled data for these purposes is highly desirable, especially in semi-supervised and self-supervised learning scenarios, as comprehensively surveyed by Qu et al. (2022) and demonstrated by methods like SelfMatch (Kim et al., 2021).

strengths: The core idea of 'local inconsistency' as a generalization measure is highly novel and offers a fresh perspective on understanding and improving generalization in deep learning. Its derivation from information-geometry and connection to FIM is theoretically elegant.

The ability to compute local inconsistency using *only unlabeled data* and a *single trained model* is a significant practical advantage, especially in semi-supervised and self-supervised learning, addressing a major limitation of prior inconsistency-based measures.

The proposed Inconsistency-Aware Minimization (IAM) framework demonstrates strong empirical performance across various learning paradigms (supervised, semi-supervised, and self-supervised), often matching or exceeding state-of-the-art methods like SAM, showcasing its broad applicability and potential impact.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the generalization bound (Theorem 1, informal) relies on a heuristic assumption (Equation 13) that 'the worst-case increase in empirical loss is approximately proportional to local inconsistency'. While intuitively plausible, a more rigorous derivation or empirical validation of this proportionality would strengthen the paper's theoretical foundation.

The empirical evaluation, while comprehensive across tasks, could benefit from a deeper analysis of the trade-offs involved in selecting hyperparameters like ρ and β, and how these choices influence the behavior of IAM compared to SAM. More sensitivity analyses would be valuable.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper introduces 'local inconsistency,' a novel generalization measure rooted in information geometry, which is a bold and innovative idea. While the theoretical generalization bound is somewhat heuristic, the conceptual novelty and strong empirical results make this work highly significant. It opens up exciting new avenues for research into generalization and optimization in deep learning, especially for data-scarce scenarios. The minor theoretical imperfections do not detract from the overall strength and potential impact of this forward-looking research.

paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection via Variational Auto-Encoder for Seasonal KPIs in Web Applications
paper_metadata.abstract: To ensure undisrupted business, large Internet companies need to closely monitor various KPIs (e.g., Page Views, number of online users, and number of orders) of its Web applications, to accurately detect anomalies and trigger timely troubleshooting/mitigation. However, anomaly detection for these seasonal KPIs with various patterns and data quality has been a great challenge, especially without labels. In this paper, we proposed Donut, an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm based on VAE. Thanks to a few of our key techniques, Donut greatly outperforms a state-of-arts supervised ensemble approach and a baseline VAE approach, and its best F-scores range from 0.75 to 0.9 for the studied KPIs from a top global Internet company. We come up with a novel KDE interpretation of reconstruction for Donut, making it the first VAE-based anomaly detection algorithm with solid theoretical explanation.

paper_metadata.title: DeepAnT: A Deep Learning Approach for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Time Series
paper_metadata.abstract: Traditional distance and density-based anomaly detection techniques are unable to detect periodic and seasonality related point anomalies which occur commonly in streaming data, leaving a big gap in time series anomaly detection in the current era of the IoT. To address this problem, we present a novel deep learning-based anomaly detection approach (DeepAnT) for time series data, which is equally applicable to the non-streaming cases. DeepAnT is capable of detecting a wide range of anomalies, i.e., point anomalies, contextual anomalies, and discords in time series data. In contrast to the anomaly detection methods where anomalies are learned, DeepAnT uses unlabeled data to capture and learn the data distribution that is used to forecast the normal behavior of a time series. DeepAnT consists of two modules: time series predictor and anomaly detector. The time series predictor module uses deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict the next time stamp on the defined horizon. This module takes a window of time series (used as a context) and attempts to predict the next time stamp. The predicted value is then passed to the anomaly detector module, which is responsible for tagging the corresponding time stamp as normal or abnormal. DeepAnT can be trained even without removing the anomalies from the given data set. Generally, in deep learning-based approaches, a lot of data are required to train a model. Whereas in DeepAnT, a model can be trained on relatively small data set while achieving good generalization capabilities due to the effective parameter sharing of the CNN. As the anomaly detection in DeepAnT is unsupervised, it does not rely on anomaly labels at the time of model generation. Therefore, this approach can be directly applied to real-life scenarios where it is practically impossible to label a big stream of data coming from heterogeneous sensors comprising of both normal as well as anomalous points. We have performed a detailed evaluation of 15 algorithms on 10 anomaly detection benchmarks, which contain a total of 433 real and synthetic time series. Experiments show that DeepAnT outperforms the state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods in most of the cases, while performing on par with others.

paper_metadata.title: A Hybrid Deep Learning Anomaly Detection Framework for Intrusion Detection
paper_metadata.abstract: Cyber intrusion attacks that compromise the users' critical and sensitive data are escalating in volume and intensity, especially with the growing connections between our daily life and the Internet. The large volume and high complexity of such intrusion attacks have impeded the effectiveness of most traditional defence techniques. While at the same time, the remarkable performance of the machine learning methods, especially deep learning, in computer vision, had garnered research interests from the cyber security community to further enhance and automate intrusion detections. However, the expensive data labeling and limitation of anomalous data make it challenging to train an intrusion detector in a fully supervised manner. Therefore, intrusion detection based on unsupervised anomaly detection is an important feature too. In this paper, we propose a three-stage deep learning anomaly detection based network intrusion attack detection framework. The framework comprises an integration of unsupervised (K-means clustering), semi-supervised (GANomaly) and supervised learning (CNN) algorithms. We then evaluated and showed the performance of our implemented framework on three benchmark datasets: NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2018, and TON_IoT.

paper_metadata.title: Anomaly Detection of Tabular Data Using LLMs
paper_metadata.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown their potential in long-context understanding and mathematical reasoning. In this paper, we study the problem of using LLMs to detect tabular anomalies and show that pre-trained LLMs are zero-shot batch-level anomaly detectors. That is, without extra distribution-specific model fitting, they can discover hidden outliers in a batch of data, demonstrating their ability to identify low-density data regions. For LLMs that are not well aligned with anomaly detection and frequently output factual errors, we apply simple yet effective data-generating processes to simulate synthetic batch-level anomaly detection datasets and propose an end-to-end fine-tuning strategy to bring out the potential of LLMs in detecting real anomalies. Experiments on a large anomaly detection benchmark (ODDS) showcase i) GPT-4 has on-par performance with the state-of-the-art transductive learning-based anomaly detection methods and ii) the efficacy of our synthetic dataset and fine-tuning strategy in aligning LLMs to this task.

paper_metadata.title: New Methods and Datasets for Group Anomaly Detection From Fundamental Physics
paper_metadata.abstract: The identification of anomalous overdensities in data - group or collective anomaly detection - is a rich problem with a large number of real world applications. However, it has received relatively little attention in the broader ML community, as compared to point anomalies or other types of single instance outliers. One reason for this is the lack of powerful benchmark datasets. In this paper, we first explain how, after the Nobel-prize winning discovery of the Higgs boson, unsupervised group anomaly detection has become a new frontier of fundamental physics (where the motivation is to find new particles and forces). Then we propose a realistic synthetic benchmark dataset (LHCO2020) for the development of group anomaly detection algorithms. Finally, we compare several existing statistically-sound techniques for unsupervised group anomaly detection, and demonstrate their performance on the LHCO2020 dataset.

paper_metadata.title: Fine-grained Anomaly Detection via Multi-task Self-Supervision
paper_metadata.abstract: Detecting anomalies using deep learning has become a major challenge over the last years, and is becoming increasingly promising in several fields. The introduction of self-supervised learning has greatly helped many methods including anomaly detection where simple geometric transformation recognition tasks are used. However these methods do not perform well on fine-grained problems since they lack finer features. By combining in a multi-task framework high-scale shape features oriented task with low-scale fine features oriented task, our method greatly improves fine-grained anomaly detection. It outperforms state-of-the-art with up to 31% relative error reduction measured with AUROC on various anomaly detection problems.

paper_metadata.title: Representation Learning in Anomaly Detection: Successes, Limits and a Grand Challenge
paper_metadata.abstract: In this perspective paper, we argue that the dominant paradigm in anomaly detection cannot scale indefinitely and will eventually hit fundamental limits. This is due to the a no free lunch principle for anomaly detection. These limitations can be overcome when there are strong tasks priors, as is the case for many industrial tasks. When such priors do not exists, the task is much harder for anomaly detection. We pose two such tasks as grand challenges for anomaly detection: i) scientific discovery by anomaly detection ii) a "mini-grand" challenge of detecting the most anomalous image in the ImageNet dataset. We believe new anomaly detection tools and ideas would need to be developed to overcome these challenges.

rag_package.related_work_summary: Fully unsupervised anomaly detection is a critical challenge, particularly given the prohibitive cost of obtaining labeled anomaly data. Early work in this area includes Unsupervised Anomaly Detection via Variational Auto-Encoder for Seasonal KPIs in Web Applications (Xu et al., 2018) which leverages VAEs for unsupervised anomaly detection in seasonal KPIs, and DeepAnT: A Deep Learning Approach for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Time Series (Munir et al., 2018) which introduces a deep learning method for unsupervised time series anomaly detection. More recently, A Hybrid Deep Learning Anomaly Detection Framework for Intrusion Detection (Kale et al., 2022) proposed a multi-stage framework integrating unsupervised methods and evaluated it on various benchmark datasets. While some approaches like Fine-grained Anomaly Detection via Multi-task Self-Supervision (Jezequel et al., 2021) explore self-supervised learning, the field faces fundamental limits, as discussed in Representation Learning in Anomaly Detection: Successes, Limits and a Grand Challenge (Hoshen, 2023). Benchmark datasets, such as those proposed in New Methods and Datasets for Group Anomaly Detection From Fundamental Physics (Kasieczka et al., 2021), are crucial for advancing this area. The application of large language models for tabular anomaly detection, as shown in Anomaly Detection of Tabular Data Using LLMs (Li et al., 2024), demonstrates novel directions, but the core challenge of fully unsupervised detection across diverse domains remains.

3.desc: No RAG, 2 iterations, 1 reviewer, AI Detector enabled, no author rebuttal

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel approach by applying the Knowledge Distillation (KD) paradigm to the challenging Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) setting, which has been largely unexplored in this context. The core idea of mitigating 'anomaly interference' through cross-domain distillation is genuinely innovative and pushes the boundaries of current UAD methods.

The proposed Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework, with its Domain-Specific Training (DST) and Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation (CDKA) components, is conceptually strong and well-reasoned. The assumptions driving the design (Limited Representation of Rare Anomalies, Lack of Cross-Anomaly Generalization) provide a solid theoretical foundation for the practical solution.

The empirical results demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing baselines and FUAD methods, particularly in the more challenging 'Overlap' setting where anomaly noise in the training data is directly tested. This validates the effectiveness and robustness of the CDD framework in real-world scenarios.
weaknesses: While the approach is novel, the empirical evaluation primarily focuses on the MVTec AD and VisA datasets. Exploring its applicability and performance on a wider range of datasets or different types of anomalies could further solidify its generality and robustness.

The paper mentions that the core design is conceptually general and could be extended to other UAD paradigms but restricts experiments to RD-based architectures. A brief discussion or some preliminary experiments on other paradigms would have strengthened the claim of generality, even if not fully validated.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly novel and significant contribution to the field of anomaly detection by pioneering the use of Knowledge Distillation in the Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) setting. The core idea of mitigating anomaly interference through a cross-domain distillation framework is highly innovative and well-justified by detailed theoretical assumptions. While there are minor methodological imperfections, such as the limited scope of experimental validation to only RD-based architectures, the potential impact of this work is immense. The improvements shown over baselines in challenging noisy environments are compelling and demonstrate its practical utility. This work boldly pushes the field forward, laying a strong foundation for future research in FUAD with KD, and thus, I wholeheartedly recommend its acceptance. The author did not provide a rebuttal, which is understandable given the strong initial review, and my assessment remains unchanged.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel and creative approach by extending Knowledge Distillation to the challenging Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) setting, a direction previously underexplored with KD.

The core idea of 'fence off anomaly interference' through Domain-Specific Training and Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation is ingenious. Partitioning data and strategically aggregating knowledge from domain-specific students to guide a global student is a fresh perspective on handling noisy training data in anomaly detection.

The two assumptions (Limited Representation of Rare Anomalies and Lack of Cross-Anomaly Generalization) are well-articulated and provide a strong theoretical grounding for the proposed methods, which sets the stage for a truly innovative solution.
weaknesses: While the experimental results show significant improvements, the evaluation could benefit from multi-run statistics (e.g., error bars) to confirm the robustness of the reported performance, especially given the dynamic nature of the method (e.g., dynamic K). The authors explain the computational constraints, which is understandable, but remains an area for strengthening.

The reliance on assumptions about anomaly distribution (limited representation, lack of cross-generalization) is central to the method. While the authors' response clarifies the indirect empirical evidence, a more direct empirical validation or a deeper dive into the theoretical bounds of these assumptions, even if limited by the FUAD setting, would further solidify the paper's claims.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly bold and innovative approach to Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) by pioneering the application of Knowledge Distillation. The concept of 'Cross-Domain Distillation' to mitigate anomaly interference in noisy training sets is highly novel and very exciting. The proposed Domain-Specific Training and Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation, rooted in well-reasoned assumptions, represent a creative and forward-thinking solution. The authors' rebuttal provides a reasonable explanation regarding the computational constraints for multi-run statistics and elaborates on the indirect empirical evidence for their assumptions. They've committed to a more explicit discussion in a revised version on how the ablative components connect to and validate the underlying assumptions. While the absence of direct empirical validation for assumptions and multi-run statistics are noted, I find the argument for indirect evidence and the practical constraints in the FUAD setting to be acceptable. The fundamental novelty and significant potential impact of this method remain very strong. This work pushes the boundaries of what is possible in FUAD and opens up new avenues for research, making it a valuable contribution to the field.

strengths: The paper introduces a highly novel and creative approach to Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) by leveraging the Knowledge Distillation (KD) paradigm in a cross-domain manner. This is a significant conceptual leap for FUAD, which has largely relied on memory-bank based methods.

The core idea of reducing anomaly interference through 'Domain-Specific Training' and 'Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation' is brilliant. The two assumptions (Limited Representation of Rare Anomalies and Lack of Cross-Anomaly Generalization) provide a solid theoretical motivation for the proposed mechanism.

The experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing FUAD methods, especially in challenging 'Overlap' settings and with increasing noise ratios. This robust performance validates the effectiveness of the proposed CDD framework.
weaknesses: While the theoretical assumptions are well-justified, the empirical validation of these assumptions (e.g., explicitly showing that domain-specific students fail to generalize to out-of-domain anomaly patterns) could be more thoroughly explored, perhaps with more detailed feature space visualizations.

The sensitivity analysis and optimization of these parameters are somewhat limited, especially the dynamic K strategy which offers improvements but its rationale could be further elaborated beyond a single example.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a truly innovative and forward-thinking approach to Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection. By cleverly adapting Knowledge Distillation and introducing a novel cross-domain strategy, it tackles the critical problem of anomaly interference in noisy training data. The core ideas of Domain-Specific Training and Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation are highly creative and theoretically grounded in two intuitive assumptions. Although there could be more in-depth empirical validation of these assumptions and a broader hyperparameter analysis, the demonstrated performance improvements, particularly in challenging scenarios, strongly indicate the significance and potential impact of this work. It pushes the boundaries of FUAD beyond conventional memory-bank methods and opens up new avenues for research in this area. This bold concept, even with minor imperfections, is exactly what we need to advance the field.

strengths: The paper rigorously tackles the challenging and practical problem of Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) where training data contains unlabeled anomalies, which is a crucial aspect for real-world deployment.

The proposed Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework is well-motivated by two key assumptions (Limited Representation of Rare Anomalies and Lack of Cross-Anomaly Generalization), which are formally described with equations and provide a solid theoretical basis for the method's design choices.

The evaluation is comprehensive, conducting experiments on two standard datasets (MVTec AD and VisA) under both 'No Overlap' and 'Overlap' settings with varying anomaly ratios. The ablation studies effectively demonstrate the contribution of each proposed module and design parameter (e.g., number of domains, selection of pseudo-normal features).

The method demonstrates significant quantitative improvements over a strong baseline (RD) and other FUAD methods, particularly in pixel-level localization and robustness to higher anomaly noise ratios, addressing a critical limitation of previous KD-based approaches in FUAD.
weaknesses: While the theoretical assumptions (Assumption 1 and 2) are stated, they rely on empirical observations (e.g., P(N) >> P(Am)) without deeper mathematical proofs or bounds on when these assumptions hold true, which could strengthen the formal soundness.

The paper mentions that the core design is conceptually general but experiments are restricted to RD-based architectures. While this is noted as future work, a brief discussion or initial exploration of how it might apply to one other UAD paradigm (e.g., reconstruction-based) would reinforce the claim of generality.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a well-structured and rigorously evaluated approach to Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection. The core idea of using cross-domain distillation to 'fence off anomaly interference' is sound, and the two major assumptions underpin a logical set of design choices. The experimental results clearly demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed CDD framework, particularly its ability to outperform baselines and other FUAD methods under challenging noisy training conditions across multiple metrics and datasets. The ablation studies are thorough and effectively validate the contribution of individual components. Although the theoretical underpinnings could be further formalized with more rigorous proofs for the stated assumptions, and a broader application beyond RD architectures would be beneficial, the current work represents a strong technical contribution to the field. The detailed experimental setup, performance analysis, and discussions make a convincing case for the method's validity and utility.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and relevant problem (FUAD) using a knowledge distillation paradigm, which is crucial for real-world industrial applications where anomalous data is inevitable during training.

The proposed Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework, particularly the Domain-Specific Training and Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation, provides a well-reasoned and empirically supported approach to mitigate anomaly interference during training.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering two challenging FUAD settings ('No Overlap' and 'Overlap') on MVTec AD and VisA datasets, demonstrating significant performance improvements over strong baselines, including a detailed ablation study.
weaknesses: While the paper justifies its focus on RD, the generalization of CDD to other UAD paradigms is only discussed conceptually rather than explicitly demonstrated, limiting its immediate practical scope to KD-based methods.

The dynamic adjustment strategy for 'K' (number of domains) in the ablation study is interesting ('{2,3,3,2}' achieving the best PRO), but the heuristic behind this specific sequence or a more principled way to determine 'K' is not fully elaborated, which could impact reproducibility or tuning in new scenarios.
